speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour and privilege to present a petition on behalf
of residents of Scarborough, Don Mills, North York, and Toronto who join with thousands of supporters and volunteers in supporting the Rouge Valley in Scarborough as a unique and precious natural area.

They point out that on October 30, 1987, the then Minister of State for Immigration promised unmarried sons and daughters of all ages would be considered as members of the family class of immigrants, that married children and brothers and sisters in the assisted relative class would get 15 points instead of 10 points.

Therefore they call upon the House to ensure that the Government will fulfil its promise now.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a number of petitions from my riding and other ridings in the Greater Vancouver region. As well, there are over 100 names from Ottawa, Scarborough, Etobicoke and Toronto.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to move on to debate today the Government's position on Bill C-84. As I have said frequently, Bill C-84 forms with Bill C-55 a complementary package that will create a fair, effective way of ensuring that the rights of genuine refugees and our international obligations are respected.
Equally important, we must take the necessary legislative steps to ensure that abuse of the system does not occur.

Bill C-84 must be passed without delay so that the attempts that have repeatedly been made to abuse the refugee determination process can be counteracted. The passage of Bill C-84 is also necessary to ensure that the measures proposed in Bill C-55 will be effective once they are put in place. That is why I consider these two Bills to be a legislative package.
Madam Speaker, I would like to note that one of the controversial points in Bill C-84 was the empowering of the Minister to order ships turned back on the high seas if they were transporting people who hoped to claim refugee status in Canada. Today I want to announce a sunset clause that will do away with this power six months after the passage of Bill C-55.

I just want to make it clear that we are proposing a sunset clause that will eliminate the power to turn away ships six months after proclamation of Bill C-55. In the interim, the Government is also proposing an amendment limiting the power to turn back ships to those carrying illegal migrants which are intercepted outside our 12-mile limit. In addition, we are proposing, for consistency with Bill C-55, that only the Minister will be able to exclude security risks from Canada.
The Government believes that the deterrent measures in Bill C-84 provide ample power to discourage the increasing abuse of our refugee determination system. These measures include increased penalties for the organizers of illegal migration and for their accomplices, including the imposition of ten-year jail sentences and fines of $500,000; heavier fines for transportation companies that bring undocumented arrivals; increased powers to detain security risks and unidentified arrivals; exclusion of security risks and criminals from the determination process; increased powers of search and seizure; improved electronic surveillance capability.
July 12, 1988

The net result of these measures will be a refugee determination system better able to help those truly in need and to handle the unprecedented global pressures we are now facing. We will face these problems with legislation that respects the Geneva Convention, respects our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and respects our humanitarian traditions in Canada.
In conclusion, it is my hope that now that our response to Bill C-84 can be seen to be fair and reasonable the other place will see fit to move with dispatch on Bill C-85 so that we can begin the process of putting it in place.
I move:
That a Message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this House agrees with amendment 1 made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976, and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, but disagrees with amendments 2(A) and (B) and with the earlier amendments 5(B) and (C), on which the Senate insists, because this House believes they contradict the principles of the Bill for the following reasons:
Amendments 2(A) and (B) would reverse the policy on which the Immigration Act, 1976 was based, which policy was not changed in the Bill as passed by this House. The amendments jeopardize the possibility of successfully prosecuting persons who profit from organizing illegal migration and from counselling fraud among refugee claimants.
Earlier amendments 5(B) and (C) arise out of Senate amendment 5(A), which is amended by this House, and are inconsistent with that amendment.
And, that this House agrees with the principles set out in amendment 3 and in earlier amendment 5(A) on which the Senate insists, but would propose the following amendments:
Amendment 3 be amended to read as follows:
"Strike out lines 14 to 16 on page 24 and substitute the following:
Referred to in paragraphs 19(1)(E), (2)(A) and 48.1(c) and subsections 39(2), 40(1), 41(1), 82.1(2), 83(1) and 91.1(1), and any such power,"
Earlier amendment 5(A) be amended to read as follows:
"Strike out lines 13 to 30 on page 8, and substitute the following:
91.1(1) Subject to subsection (1.1), where the Minister believes on reasonable grounds that a vehicle within twelve nautical miles of the outer limit of the territorial sea of Canada is bringing any person into Canada in contravention of this Act or the regulations, the Minister may direct the vehicle not to enter the internal waters of Canada or the territorial sea of Canada, as the case may be, and any such direction may be enforced by such force as is reasonable in the circumstances.
(1.1) The Minister may make a direction under subsection (1) where the Minister is satisfied

(A)	the vehicle can return to its port of embarkation without endangering the lives of its passengers;
(B)	All passengers who seek Convention refugee status and are nationals or citizens of the country where the vehicle embarked them have been removed from the vehicle and brought into Canada;
(C)	The country where the vehicle embarked its passengers is a signatory to the Convention and complies with Article 33 thereof; and
(D)	The country would allow the passengers to return to that country or to have the merits of their claims to Convention refugee status determined therein.
(1.2) Where the minister believes on reasonable grounds that a vehicle within
(A) The internal waters of Canada, or
Immigration Act, 1976
(B) The territorial sea of Canada
Is bringing any person into Canada in contravention of this Act or the regulations, the Minister may direct that the vehicle be escorted to the nearest port of disembarkation and any such direction may be enforced by such force as is reasonably necessary."
That concludes my response, Madam Speaker. I believe if you seek the opinion of the House you will find we have unanimous consent to add an additional amendment to this Bill.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise on behalf of the Liberal caucus to respond to the latest response of the Government concerning Bill C-84 which was introduced about a year ago. I think it is fitting that on the very anniversary of the boatload of Sikh refugee claimants landing on the East Coast of our country that we would be, first, debating a Bill that was intended to be an emergency and, second, that we would be talking specifically about the whole proposal of turning back boats and the sunset clause introduced by the Minister a few moments ago.
I would also like to pay tribute to the Senators, both the Liberal Senators and government Senators, who have worked very respectfully and thoroughly in providing a forum for organizations and groups from across this country.
Now that the dust has settled with respect to the so-called emergency, the so-called crisis, the national call for Parliament to convene to pass emergency legislation, members on the government side and, indeed Canadians, have been able to

July 12, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
reflect on last summer's activities, the manipulation of the situation, and the creation of hysteria. After several months of reflection and taking a proper perspective on the situation, I believe all government Members and groups now believe that the tabling of such Draconian legislation was not only a disservice to the best traditions which define this country, a country which has offered international leadership to our partners and allies around the globe, but it was also an overkill in terms of the very proponents of the legislation contained in Bill C-84.
That is the reason that Members in this House and Members in the other place, as well as groups across this country, have tried to address what I believe is the worst performance of any government in dealing with immigration and refugee matters. I believe to call a national emergency based on 147 individuals is a shame for this Government and, unfortunately, a shame for this country.
It was only several years ago that the Government, supported by the same citizens, progressively and very courageously participated in a world-wide effort to find homes for the so-called Vietnamese boat people. This country accepted close to 106,000 Vietnamese boat people over the course of approximately a year and one-half. Half of them were sponsored by the Government and the other half were sponsored by individual communities. Only a few years later, last summer, based on 147 individuals, at a time when the Government found itself in the doldrums of the popularity polls, it moved in an unprecedented and very shameful way.
There have been efforts by Members in this House and in the other Chamber, as well as Canadians from coast to coast, to amend and ameliorate a bad piece of legislation. We tried to bring it into conformity with the standards and traditions of our country in terms of immigration and refugee policies. We did so not because, as the Government suggests, we somehow want to legitimize abuse. No one in this Chamber or in this country is in favour of illegitimate refugees, immigrants, or profiteers who simply make their living by taking advantage of desperate human beings in very difficult circumstances. No one in any part of government, whether it is a Department dealing with pensions or UIC, immigration or refugees, condones the undermining of our rules and regulations. However, having said that, nor do we consent to the stripping away of the regulations and the laws to which we adhered which took such a long time to develop and nurture. The fights and debates to get where we are in terms of our processes and in terms of our laws were not an overnight success. It was not an easy debate. In a short span of time we have sacrificed the work and the efforts of so many people and so many previous Governments. In the process we have jeopardized our reputation abroad.
Every legal expert who came before the legislative committee, the standing committee, as well as before the Senate committee, said that many clauses both in Bill C-84 and Bill
C-55 are very much unconstitutional and violate the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which we passed as a Parliament several years ago. The importance of that testimony is in terms of what will happen if the courts agree with the body of opinion presented by legal experts, a nearly unanimous opinion which predicted that if this legislation becomes law it will be challenged in the courts and the courts will uphold those challenges.
What then will the Minister say to Canadians? What then will the Government say to the country when its policies are paralysed as a result of verdicts rendered by various courts? It will then have done the country a greater disservice since in paralysing our policies in the courts public confidence will not be there. Instead of public confidence there will be public cynicism rooted in the belief that the Government was trying to correct a situation but in so doing has made it worse.
Therefore what we were trying to do-and we make no bones about it-was to prevent a piece of legislation from being tied up in the courts and in the result having our system undermined by a court decision. One of the fundamental, if not the foremost, priorities as a Parliament is to draft good legislation, legislation that is in keeping with the first law of the land, our Constitution. If we have doubts about a law's constitutionality, or if we have doubts about the Department of Justice not being in accord with the Department of Immigration, and if we have not seen the justice opinion, if the Government has not had the courage to show its critics and cynics that the decision was rooted on sound judicial ground, then we have an obligation as a Parliament to try to correct that flawed legislation.
In the Minister's response of a few moments ago we saw the same inflexibility that she demonstrated in her response to Bill C-55. When she responded to Bill C-55 it was as a new Minister of Employment and Immigration. She is now somewhat more seasoned. She has had an opportunity to grasp a very difficult portfolio. No one pretends that this portfolio is an easy one with which to contend. However, in the Minister's response we see the same business-as-usual attitude. In her response to Bill C-84 she has failed to break the log-jam concerning two critical areas of concern. The first area of concern is the question with respect to turning back a boat. However, at the end of her remarks today she added an interesting and puzzling footnote with respect to a sunset clause on which I will comment later.
The real stumbling block for most Canadians was caused by the provision to turn a boat back and the aiding and abetting provision whereby individuals and church organizations, including priests and nuns who may be helping refugees come into Canada, will face a potential fine or imprisonment. Those were the two hang-ups that the country had with Bill C-84. Rather than try to ameliorate the two in a real fashion the Minister has chosen to ignore the testimony, the articulate, emotional and passionate pleas that organizations have made for months on end. As well she has rejected the compromises
July 12, 1988

that were put forward by the Senate in its last response to Bill C-84.
The present Minister is the fourth Conservative Minister to hold the portfolio of immigration. There were expectations that she might bring a more moderate view to the Ministry, that she might be more open and flexible to a Canadian compromise in order to de-escalate the polarized views created by this legislation. There is disappointment that she has been unwilling to tackle head on these two very fundamental and serious shortcomings in Bill C-84.
I compliment the Minister on her acceptance of the first and third amendments proposed by the Senate which at the very least in an eleventh hour compromise suggests that if the Government is to refuse any individual entry into the refugee determination process on the grounds of a security threat the Minister is the only person able to bar that individual proceeding through the process. Before this legislation any official was able to exclude an individual. The Minister has accepted a compromise, an eleventh hour suggestion from the Senate which states that only the Minister's signature will be an authorization for a person to be excluded.
I would ask the Minister to be concerned with the proposal which would exclude individuals from the refugee determination process based on information we may receive from other Governments. I also point out that Belgium is the only country in the western world which rejects individuals based on security information provided by other Governments. I would ask the Minister to be concerned about information we may receive from other Governments.
After all, what constitutes a security risk or a security threat in the eyes of another Government? If South Africa were to provide our government officials with evidence that Nelson Mandela was a subversive, a law-breaker in South Africa, then would that constitute barring Nelson Mandela from our refugee determination process? I use that example to suggest that many individuals who may be political refugees and who escape the country of their torture or their harassment may be pursued by those very same government officials who pushed them to seek refugee status in the first place.
Political refugees are the worst public relations campaign for any country. Therefore if we have political refugees who come to this country or others then we can bet our bottom dollar that the countries from which they are running will disavow the refugees' claims these individuals will make. The Governments of the countries from which these individuals flee will try to discredit and undermine those individuals who in the eyes of a dictatorship or a military regime bring instability and pressure as well as media and world attention to their policies.
That is why I moved an amendment during the debate at third reading which suggested that if the Government feared that someone was a security threat, then it should not listen to the advice of some government abroad or information that
Immigration Act, 1976
came to it via a number of different foreign sources, but rather it should issue a security certificate which would be reviewed by the Security and Intelligence Review Committee. Automatically SIRC would conduct an oral hearing, and the Cabinet would be able to argue the case in front of SIRC that this individual is a security threat. If it can be proven at that particular hearing that this individual is a security threat given the proper protections, then this individual will be removed from our country and forbidden re-entry. That would be a guarantee that foreign governments would not provide fraudulent information upon which we would exclude this individual from the refugee process. I draw that information and concern to the attention of the Minister now that she will have the sole privilege of disallowing individuals from participating in the refugee process in Canada.
Amendment number two from the Senate concerned the aiding and abetting section. Unfortunately, the Government refused to budge on the Senate compromise and on the repeated concerns of the Senate and other groups and individuals in the House who were attempting to convince the Government that it would be morally unjust and legally obscene to fine or imprison individuals from churches and organizations who assist refugees with resettling in Canada. The Government proposes to make it an offence against the person who counsels or advises the individual with improper or illegitimate travel documents and the person advising that individual may face criminal prosecution. The Senate attempted to convince the Government to make it an offence for individuals, or members of churches or organizations who counsel unfounded cases with no credible basis, or who counsel in a clandestine manner.
The operative phrase in the Government's legislation now becomes the whole question of travel documents. The Government is saying if an individual does not have proper travel documents and is assisted by an organization, a priest, or a nun to come into this country, then those people assisting the individual will now face imprisonment or a fine.
I would like to point out to the Government that that is going in the wrong direction. A legitimate refugee is more inclined to not have correct documentation. A true refugee who is facing abuse or torture will not have had the luxury or the time to go to an embassy or consulate and pick up the appropriate visa before coming to Canada. If a person is fleeing a military or dictator regime that is harassing this individual then it might be incumbent upon this legitimate refugee to make an illegitimate travel document in order that they can escape the country of torture and abuse as a first step to entering Canada.
We have suggested that in most cases legitimate refugees would be the ones who do not possess real travel documents, but yet they possess a real refugee claim. Fake refugees may be coached into having the appropriate travel documents, but do not have a legitimate case for refugee status, particularly if they are being coached by those who are professional in the art

July 12, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
of manipulation and of profiteering from individuals who face difficult circumstances abroad.
Therefore, why penalize churches or organizations that may be assisting an individual to come into the country? Regardless of the travel documents that he or she may be carrying with them, why penalize those legitimate elements in society who have tried to lend a hand and provide a bridge and a home to those who are fleeing and who are homeless?
Churches have been at the forefront of feeding the hungry through food banks, finding homes for those who live on streets or in parks, assisting senior citizens, the disadvantaged, and the poor. Why penalize those elements in churches and organizations who try to help another worthy cause, namely, those fleeing from persecutions and who are trying to find what you and I have, Madam Speaker, and what we all too often take for granted?
The Minister and the Government have said: "Don't worry. We will never use this particular clause against a church. We will never fine a priest. We will never imprison a nun. We will never undermine an organization that is legitimate". That is not how laws are constructed in this country. Legislation is not passed based on the intentions of one Minister. Today what might be the good intentions of a Minister, tomorrow might be the bad intentions of another Minister, or in 10 years' time from now. We in the House must debate and pass legislation, and analyse that legislation based on the force of this law or of the proposed law, and on the legal force and letter of this proposed law it would be criminal to persist in justifying the indefensible, and in defending and promoting that this piece of legislation should be getting the support of this Parliament and the other place.
I regret that the relatively new Minister did not have the moral fortitude to admit that that clause is onerous, offensive, and is a slap in the face to those voluntary organizations that do not have any malice or criminal intent, and have no profiteering intent, but simply try to lend a helping hand to those whom they feel are deserving of that assistance. Rather than encouraging and applauding those efforts, the Government is potentially prepared to penalize those important efforts across the country.
The other amendment that the Minister refused to accept from the Senate was amendment No. 4. This clause allows the Government to turn ships around. In amendment No. 4 the Senate attempted to amend this very sensitive clause by having the Government recognize that, if it wanted to discourage those captains and profiteers and that type of manipulative business, then the ship must be escorted into port. This would provide the opportunity to impound the boat, sell it, and proceed with prosecution of the captain for having dumped a human cargo off a coastline of our country, or attempting to subvert our regulations and laws. That would send a clear message across the Atlantic or the Pacific. If there was another captain who was prepared to set sail with another human cargo, that captain would think twice when hearing the
news that another captain or his friend lost his boat and is now facing a fine or imprisonment. That would be the deterrent that we would be looking at as a country and as a Parliament.
Instead, the Government, in refusing amendment No. 4, continues to argue that the deterrent would be to turn back the boat. I suggest that that is not the case. If you were to simply turn back a boat on which you or I were the captain, then what is the risk involved for us as a captain navigating that ship? Assuming that we collected the cash from those individuals for that Atlantic or Pacific journey, we would have the money in our pockets and 50 per cent says that we will dump the people on the coastline successively and, at the very worst, the other 50 per cent risk is that the Coast Guard finds out and turns the boat back, without even looking at who is on board, but simply turns it back.
What is the big risk for the captain? He has his money. He either dumps the human cargo further offshore or returns them to the point of departure or brings them to another country. There is nothing to lose for the captain because he has made his dollars and, indeed, has probably made big dollars.
The Government wants to discourage these manipulators, as it should, by throwing the law book at them with all the force and determination. We urge it to bring the boats in, impound them, and charge the captains. That will send a strong message. Instead, how did the Government respond? Not only did it say that it would be better to simply turn the boats around, but it began to define what areas of the sea it would be doing it in.
For instance, the Government, in the response just tabled by the Minister, suggests that between 12 and 24 nautical miles it can turn back a boat if it is satisfied with four conditions. One of the conditions is the seaworthiness of the boat and the fact of there being no danger to the lives.
Now, how are they going to make that determination 12 to 24 miles out at sea? If it is foggy and raining and the waters are choppy, what are they going to send; the Minister in a boat to determine how seaworthy the ship is? How are we going to see the condition of the ship? How are we going to make a determination concerning who is on the boat or what the health of those passengers is or how much food or water is left on that boat if we turn them around? What we are talking about is a very illogical determination that we have to make, almost impossibly, out at sea. That is what is being asked for in this one clause.
The second condition is to suggest that passengers who seek conventional refugee status and are nationals or citizens of the country from which the ship departed are removed from the boat and brought in. What do we do then? Again, in the middle of the night, we send a boat out to sea and we ask for identification. What if there is no identification, no travel documents, and people suggest that they came from a certain country and that they are nationals of a certain country, or lie
July 12, 1988

or mislead simply to get onshore? How are government officials supposed to validate who is from where and when, out at sea in the middle of the night?
The third condition is to suggest that if there are individuals on that boat who come from countries which participate in the Geneva Convention, then those people should be sent back and not be removed by the boat. How do you manage to make that determination by going through the boat in the middle of an evening with perhaps documentation that is not up to par? A boat goes out, brings back some people and a determination is made that these are individuals who are nationals from countries which do face refugee problems. They leave the rest on board based on another determination saying: "Well, you come from a country where you have your own refugee process and you respect the Convention, so we are sending you back." How can they verify on the spot, at that moment, out at sea who is who?
The fourth condition is to suggest that they are going to allow the people to go back if the country they are coming from will allow them to return. Again, what are they going to do? If people on the boat say: "Well, I come from Belgium, I come from Argentina", what is the Minister going to do? Will she call the Ministers in Argentina and Belgium overnight and say: "Are you going to allow these people to return?" How are they going to make a determination at sea regarding which country and which Government will allow a person to return? To return means nothing. It does not mean to admit. There is no legal force in having a person return. That could simply mean return them to the country and the shore, keep them at the airport or the port and then send them packing.
The real problem in all these four conditions is how do you make a determination in the middle of the sea, between 12 and 24 miles, after you have stopped a boat, that these four conditions are being lived up to? How can any Government pretend to be satisfied by incorporating these four conditions concerning turning back a boat? These four conditions are an insult to people's intelligence in this Chamber and across the country. I would suggest that no government official would dare try to verify these four conditions in the middle of the sea, 12 to 24 nautical miles outside of this country. It is simply incredible. They are passing it off as legitimate proposals.
The Minister should have a serious rethinking and reevaluation and not try to pass off the very humorous-they are not even that. They are serious. If this is going to become the legislation of this country, it is going to be very serious and indeed a shame to try to make these conditions verifiable in the middle of the sea.
Then they talk about internal waters. Concerning internal waters and up to 12 miles, they basically have the same philosophy. In that particular amendment, the Government is saying that between our internal waters and 12 miles the Government may bring a ship into port. Well, the word "may", of course, is very weak. It means, by the same token, that a ship within those waters may be turned around as well.
Immigration Act, 1976
If you are going to turn them around between zero and 12 miles, where are the conditions? You do not have conditions, first, and second, if you did have conditions, as badly and as poorly and as illogically drafted as the first set of conditions, then those are not a safeguard in terms of trying to validate who is on board, whether the passengers are refugees, whether they are safe, and to impound the boat and fine and imprison the captain.
The Government, while trying to define between 12 miles and 24 miles on four flimsy conditions, is really saying the same thing: "Give us the power to turn boats around". The Senate is suggesting, and we are suggesting that that is not the answer to illegitimate smugglers, because it does not offer a penalty harsh enough, because you cannot get the captain or will not be able to impound the boat, and second, how do you process potential refugees on a boat? How do you turn that boat around? How do you allow those people to return when you do not even know if they are going to be returning to face continued persecution or possible death?
Therefore, the logical and humane thing to do would be to accept the boat and escort it under Canadian supervision into our port, allow the cases to be processed and allow the captain and the boat to be penalized to the extreme. That would be the solution rather than the response that the Government has proposed to us this morning, which I believe is very silly and in essence saying the same thing by using different legislative language.
Concerning the zero to 12 miles the Government uses the language "may bring a ship into port". I will be moving an amendment at the end of my comments to change the word "may" to "shall". At least within internal orders and up to 12 miles the law of the land will be that if you see a boat you will bring it into port, not return it, but "shall bring it into port" so you will offer the processing and the punishment that should be facing the captain and crew.
The Government through the Minister a few moments ago moved a very puzzling and seductive sunset clause. After just arguing the case for turning back a boat, after the sophistication of between zero and 12 miles and 12 to 24 miles, after a full year of the Government defending the absolute need for turning back boats, the Minister now says that the Government will be prepared to consider a sunset clause. The Government is saying that if Parliament gives us Bill C-55, the Government will drop the turning back the boat provision six months after that legislation comes into force. The big question is why do that at this stage. If you accept the point that you need two pieces of legislation, one for reforming the processing-which is Bill C-55-and one for discouraging smugglers, why after arguing for a year does one at the eleventh hour, after offering the stick and carrot routine to the Senate, let go of the carrot? Something is wrong.

July 12, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Either the Government could have admitted that turning back the boat was a very wrong and misguided provision or the Government could have defended it, if that is what the Government wanted to do. Instead the Government has chosen perhaps the worst of all possibilities. It has defended its right to the end today by rejecting amendment No. 4. It then offered the carrot by saying if you give us Bill C-55, we will strike that provision from the books. It is a very seducing carrot that I do not regard as completely being respectful. The Government is mixing the two Bills and is using potential lives at sea as the bargaining chips for it to get through the Elouse and Parliament another piece of legislation. That is bargaining of the lowest kind.
When the Government accepted the principles of having a deterrence and a processing Bill, we advocated that if those two went together we would have one Bill, striking the clause of turning back the boats because that is a wrong direction for this country to go on refugee legislation. If the Government is interested in making that seducing deal with the other place, and it is trying to get Bill C-55 through so it can strike the provision, why make a deal in terms of the provisions in Bill C-55 where there is inflexibility?
If you accept at this stage that you will not be able to turn back boats, why did the Government not accept that principle a year ago when we urged it not to have that provision and urged the Government to have people processed as the Government will have us do if and when Bill C-55 becomes legislation? The Government will now strike the provision. I too would want that provision struck from our laws and books. One can argue that even if this is a very immoral way of bargaining, using people as leverage to try to strike a provision that was wrong from the first, it would still be laudable to have that provision off the books. I am also asking at what price and at what cost is the Government asking us to do it and in what manner is the Government trying to strike it from the books by trading it with another piece of legislation rather than having the principle and the gumption to stand up and say that that particular clause is wrong, we will eradicate it; there are no conditions; there are no strings attached; it will not become part of our legislation?
While I do not want to see that provision in the law books of the country, I find it very disturbing the Government would use desperate people as leverage to strike something that was wrong to start with.
We still have two onerous provisions; aiding and abetting and the turning back of the boats. In terms of aiding and abetting, it is useful to remind ourselves of the words spoken by Nancy Pocock from the Inter-church Committee for Refugees. She was recently given a prestigious award for her work in the area of refugees. She said:
If my Government tells me it is a crime to help these people, I will have to say I am obeying a higher law and I am going to continue to help them when they need me.
We should think about that, Madam Speaker. We should also think about the words spoken by Mr. George Cram also from the Inter-church Committee for Refugees. He spoke about turning back boats and said:
When we had the boat crisis in 1979, we went and saw boats being pushed off the coast of Malaysia. We saw boats being pushed off various countries around the Southeast Asia and we saw refugees dying. Why? Because the boats were not allowed to land.
We are creating that. We are doing precisely what we spoke about in the United Nations in horror, that when boats carrying illegals are not allowed to land, they die.
Finally I refer to a letter that was just sent to the Minister. I believe a photocopy was sent to myself and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), the critic for the New Democratic Party. This letter reads in part:
I am very concerned about the possible passage of Bills C-55 and C-84 as they are in their present state... I also have a great fear that our international reputation for humanitarian conduct has already been somewhat eroded. At this moment, since I volunteer with the resettlement of refugee women, I am not too proud to be a Canadian. I would like to be able to hold my head up high when and after I assist these women to deal with the rules we make in this country.
I trust that you will pay attention to our concerns re. the refugee Bills. Canadians have done years of hard work to achieve for Canada its reputation as a good citizen among other countries. Let's not destroy that now!
That letter was written by Maria Lanthier of the City of Toronto.
I believe those three individual quotes summarize how we feel about this legislation. We hoped that the Minister would have amended those two onerous clauses so we could preserve a domestic system that would do us honour but at the same time would protect our international reputation as Mrs. Lanthier has so articulately spelled out in her letter. We will then continue to be leaders of good policy around the world. We would be trying to build an international resolve for strengthening rather than weakening the international leadership for assisting refugees throughout the world.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau):
That the proposed motion to amend Clause 91.1, subsection (1) of Bill C-84 be amended as follows:
"(1.1) The Minister shall make a direction under subsection (1) where the Minister is satisfied

(A)	The vehicle can return to its port of embarkation without endangering the lives of its passengers;
(B)	All passengers who seek Convention refugee status and are nationals or citizens of the country where the vehicle embarked them have been removed from the vehicle and brought into Canada;
(C)	the country where the vehicle embarked its passengers is a signatory to the Convention and complies with Article 33 thereof; and
(D)	the country would allow the passengers to return to that country or to have the merits of their claims to Convention refugee status determined therein.
(1.2) Where the Minister believes on reasonable grounds that a vehicle within
July 12, 1988

(A)	the internal waters of Canada, or
(B)	the territorial sea of Canada is bringing any person into Canada in contravention of this Act or the regulations, the Minister shall direct that vehicle to be escorted to the nearest port of disembarkation and any such direction shall be enforced by such force as is reasonably necessary."
The key change, as I articulated earlier, is to change the word "may" to the word "shall" which would have the force of ensuring that any boats within 12 miles of Canada which approach with refugee claimants will have to be brought into port so that the refugee claimants may be processed and the captain thoroughly punished, fined and imprisoned and the boat sold. In this way, we may send a real message that there is a front door for refugee determination and that those who take the back door will pay a very severe price.
That is the direction in which this Parliament should be going. That is progressive legislation for this Government to build on the success and tradition of our victories in refugee legislation. The Government should not shame them by undermining them and by tearing apart the resolve that took years of building and debating.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to speak again against Bill C-84 and particularly against the Minister's message to the Senate the second time around answering to their second attempt to reduce the wrongs of this Bill.
The Minister's message continues injustice to refugees. It continues, contrary to her opinion, to flout the United Nations Convention in the opinion of those who are expert in the matter. It continues to flout the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada that provides to everyone physically in Canada the opportunity to make a refugee claim and it continues to visit special indignity and insult and injustice on Canadians who help real refugees.
This arises out of a so-called emergency 11 months ago when about 174 dark-skinned people came in a boat to the East Coast and asked for refugee status. That was regarded as an invasion. Although the Minister preferred to talk about thousands and tens of thousands, it was 174 people with dark skins whom the Minister used as the excuse for this unjust legislation.
I will not repeat the long list of people who came as individuals or as representatives of the churches and other public bodies to testify against this Bill, and who sent letters and petitions and who organized rallies against this Bill. In contrast, none, not one came from the public to support this Bill, only the Minister and those officials who had helped to write it. The fact is that that opposition has not gone away and
Immigration Act, 1976
the Canadian Council of Churches has vowed that it will raise hundreds of thousands of dollars to make it possible to fight these Bills in court on the basis of Charter challenges.
I will point out the errors in the Minister's response. I will point out also the need that before this Bill and Bill C-55 should be proclaimed, the Minister ought to clean up the overseas refugee selection process as suggested in a report which I delivered to her yesterday morning. I will intend also to offer two amendments.
The Minister has accepted the first amendment proposed by the Senate, but unfortunately, that amendment in itself, as proposed by the Senate, introduces a new kind of injustice into what we are doing here, a new kind of injustice into the Bill. I refer to the words which say that a person may be excluded from the right to make a refugee claim if the Minister certifies that allowing him to go through the refugee process would be contrary to the public interest.
It is bad enough, as was previously being done, to say exclude him if the Minister certifies that he is a security risk. It is bad enough because there is not due process of law for that person within Canada to defend himself. But to say, as the Minister and the Senate say in Section (c), a person that they will exclude from that right guaranteed by our treaty with the United Nations, will exclude a person described in paragraphs 19(1 )(e), (f) or (g), 27(l)(c) or (2)(c), if the Minister is of the opinion that the application of Sections 45, 48, 70 and 71, the refugee process, to that person would be contrary to the public interest.
There are certain security and criminal concerns that are to be recognized and are recognized within the process that Canada agreed to 20 years ago with the United Nations that should be examined after a person has made a refugee claim and been heard, not before. But this goes much further even than the previous bad legislation proposed by the Government because this does not rest on security at all. The Government simply says: "We think it would be contrary to the public interest".
For example, if a man called Santokh Singh asks for refugee status, and if the Indian Government makes it known that it would not like it if he were given refugee status, and if Canada is seeking certain fat computer contracts with the Indian Government, then apparently it might be urged by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) that his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall), should not allow that person to make a refugee claim. It might be bad for business.
Or, for example, if the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Friesen) feels that such a person has unsatisfactory ideas, that such a person is perhaps an existentialist or belongs to some philosophical group such as the ones the Hon. Member condemned in his speech a few weeks ago, that Canada should exclude that person and that he would no doubt try to persuade the Minister to say that that person should be excluded on the

July 12, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
grounds that it would not be in the interests of the public of Canada to allow an existentialist to enter Canada. He has a lot of other people whose ideas he does not like as well, but the existentialist was the one that made even the Parliamentary Secretary laugh a few minutes ago.
This is contrary to the Charter, many of us believe, because that person in Canada has certain rights of equal treatment and due process under the Charter. Unfortunately, by the rules of order, I cannot offer an amendment to this because this was amended not by the Government but by the Senate, no doubt after consultation.
The second response to the Senate is to kill the Senate's attempt to soften the Government's section which criminalizes thousands of respected Canadians for doing what is admired by most Canadians and what has been admired by the Government of Canada and what has been admired by the United Nations High Commission for Refugees in giving Canada the Nansen Medal. They did not give it to the Government, fortunately. They gave it to the people of Canada for doing the very thing that this law would turn into a crime, helping a person, who did not already have a visa to do so, to come to Canada to claim refugee status.
It has been further demonstrated in the report I gave to the Minister's office yesterday that in places like El Salvador or Guatemala, bona fide refugees, people who have reason to fear persecution by their Governments and their death squads, are often afraid to seek a visa to enter Canada because the Canadian offices are watched by the secret police of those countries. Therefore, they have no choice but to come here without a visa. Those are the people against whom the Government has directed Bill C-84.
It has also directed the Bill against those who help those people in any sense. It has created a new offence. The Government claims it was always an offence, but that claim is patently false because no prosecution was ever attempted during the decade the existing legislation was in force. This penalty applies to people, as mentioned by my friend, such as Nancy Pocock who received the Pearson Peace Medal, who openly help these people get to the nearest Canadian Immigration Office at a point of entry to claim refugee status in spite of the fact they had not been able to get visas. This Bill creates this new offence and the Government tries to conceal that fact by claiming all it is doing is increasing the penalties. That is patently false because the penalties could have been increased without creating a new offence.
Then the Government undertakes to amend an earlier Senate amendment which it had rejected some months ago, but this time with rewording. What the Government is saying is that it wishes to allow these ships to enter under certain conditions and with certain considerations having been looked at in advance. I will not go into all of the conditions proposed in the revised 19.1(1) of the Minister, but I do wish to point to
subsection (d) where she says the Minister must be satisfied that the country to which the boat would be sent back would allow the passengers to return or to have the merits of their claim to convention refugee status determined therein. That is worthless from the point of view of saving the life of a real refugee. They can be returned to that country and the country says yes, you can return, and the next day sends them out. "Return" in immigration legal usage in this country, and that is what we have to work with, does not mean return with the right to stay.
The word "admit" means return with the right to stay, but the Government has consistently refused to allow an amendment that would use the word "admit". I will be asking again that the words "the country would allow the passengers to return to that country" be struck out and replaced with the words "the country would admit the passengers to that country". That is enough to sink the whole clause. That is, without that amendment, the error of sending them back there only with the idea they can return for an hour or a day or a week is enough to sink the whole clause and the whole law.
I wish now to come to the Minister's additional motion which, along with my hon. friend, I accepted by unanimous consent for debate. I wish to point out that with this law for turning away ships, Canada has already become an international disgrace. Canada has the gall even now to condemn Thailand for pushing boats containing refugees away from its shores, the very thing that this law insists on doing. The fact that the Minister has the common sense to say "six months later, when no one is looking, let's just quietly tow it away", may get Canada out of a bad political hole but it does not fully correct the false signals sent to the world to say Canada is now joining Thailand in pushing refugees away from our shores, legally or physically pushing them away. The most I can think of doing to amend that clause is by replacing "six months" with "one month" so that we will be correcting it very soon after C-55 has been adopted and in force, if it is adopted and in force.
I now wish to come to the points on which not only Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 fall condemned, but that there must be corrective action taken if the Minister insists on putting these into law. The effect of these laws is not only to criminalize Canadians who help refugees come to Canada to seek refugee status, but as far as possible to prevent them from doing that and to have all refugees selected overseas. Therefore, the study I commissioned examined Canada's overseas refugee selection process as it relates to Central Americans applying to our overseas offices. It finds three very grave faults in that process.
One is that it favours certain countries. I am referring here to the self-exiled person class regulation in which a person from Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, the German Democratic Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is not required to show fear of persecution. The simple fact they come from those countries is considered adequate grounds for being considered a refugee. That is discriminatory. It is unjust. It is a denial of our
July 12, 1988

obligations to the UN which require that each refugee case be considered on its merits.
There is a similar problem emerging within the region of Central America in which one country, Nicaragua, with a much better human rights record than its neighbours El Salvador and Guatemala, nevertheless has a higher acceptance rate of refugees in Canada, perhaps because they are of a more professional class. We do not know the reasons but we know the fact that there is the appearance of discrimination in favour of Nicaraguan anti-Sandanista refugees as against refugees from the fascist Government of El Salvador and the extremely repressive Government of Guatemala. This again violates our obligations to the UN.
Second, our process fails because it puts immigration considerations ahead of refugee considerations. Refugee claimants in El Salvador and Guatemala are examined first in a prescreening process to see whether Canada thinks they would be useful immigrants. If they flunk that, if they do not have medical degrees or something we would like, then they are not even allowed to state their refugee claim. This is a violation of our obligations to the UN. The prescreening used, and the sequence of interview questions used, are clearly designed to keep out many bona fide refugees and favour those who have only the slightest refugee claim but who are otherwise more desirable immigrants.
The third point is that our security requirements can delay a person for as much as a year during which time it has happened that a refugee claimant is murdered by the people he was afraid would murder him. The security requirements result in risk of physical harm to the refugee claimant and very little benefit to Canada. The RCMP testified last August that during 1986 and to that point in 1987, of 11,000 undocumented aliens that they had examined, they found no evidence of security risk or danger to Canada.
I ask the Minister to clear up these points. If she is going to insist that all our refugees be selected overseas, at least let her ensure that the system is changed to become more honest, open, fair, and in keeping with our obligations to the United Nations. I wish to move the two amendments of which I spoke. The first amendment is to Section 91.1 (1 )(d) as amended by the Government. I move:
That Section 91.1 (1 )(d) as amended by the Government be amended by deleting the words "the country would allow passengers to return to that country" and in insert therefor the words "the country would admit the passengers to that country".
The reason for that amendment is as I have mentioned. The word "admit" in our usage means that that country would allow the person to enter and stay as of right, not to be bounced out again on the next boat or the next plane.
My second amendment is to the Government's new clause. I move:
Immigration Act, 1976
That Clause 8 as amended by the Government be amended by striking out
the word "six months" and inserting therefor the words "one month".
This is an attempt to reduce the scandal caused around the world by the fact that Canada has been proposing for a year now to do what it condemns countries of Southeast Asia for doing, that is, pushing the boats away. I know there will be arguments that they are going to look after the safety of the boats and so on, but the essential point is that unless my other amendment is accepted we will be pushing away real refugees who will not then have an assured chance of having their cases examined. Since Canada has pushed them away without hearing them, Canada has no reason to expect that another country will hear them. I would ask the House to adopt both of these amendments.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a few questions I would like to ask my hon. colleague to elaborate on. The first takes us back to the genesis of this legislation. I use the word genesis advisedly because it seems to me that this legislation came about a long time ago. Last summer we were called back here in an emergency situation to deal with an urgent crisis which was facing the nation. We were called back under special Standing Orders in order to take quick action. Yet a year later we are dealing with that same legislation.
Would my colleague comment on the nature of this emergency? What kind of emergency was facing the nation which we were called back to deal with, when a full year later we are still dealing with the same legislation? Will my colleague comment on what he thinks was going on when we were called back in an emergency session a year ago and we are now still in the same session dealing with the same piece of legislation?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for a very appropriate and timely question. I will make two points in response. The nature of the emergency, as presented, was that 174 dark-skinned people had landed on the East Coast of Canada claiming refugee status. Whether they will be found to be refugees under our laws we do not yet know. The Government suggested that there would be many boats of this sort

July 12, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
coming if we did not pass a law quickly to stop them. Eleven months later no more boats have arrived. There have been rumours of boats and rumours of wars, but no more boats have arrived. Therefore, it seems that the Government over-reacted.
Second, had the Government really been interested in simply increasing penalties for people like the Captain of the Amelie, it could have done so within weeks with majority consent of the Opposition and the Canadian public. This was made known to the Government by representatives of churches, bar associations, unions, all the refugee support groups, and immigrant groups including the Canadian Ethnocultural Council. They all said that if certain amendments were accepted which focused the penalties on those who tried to bring refugees in secretly and clandestinely by deception, we would pass the legislation quickly.
The Government did not want to limit the legislation that way. It wanted to criminalize and intimidate thousands of Canadians who have been helping refugees. That is why this law has been held up today and will be held up even after it has been proclaimed because it will not stand in the courts.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have another basic question about the legislation on refugees with which we are dealing. It has to do with how people who claim to the Canadian authorities to be refugees are treated. I am wondering whether my colleague, who is informed in this area, can tell us whether when people from East European countries, for example, apply for refugee status in Canada they are treated any differently than people who apply for refugee status from Chile or El Salvador?
In other words, is the Government pursuing a uniform refugee policy or is there a significant difference in the way people from Central America are treated? I am particularly interested in knowing how someone from Chile who is applying for refugee status would be treated. We know that a young lady from Chile who stayed in Montreal had suffered serious burns as a result of political persecution under General Pinochet in Chile. She is showing great courage by going back to that country.
Can people from Chile who apply for refugee status expect equal and fair treatment as those applying from eastern European countries?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the answer to my colleague's pertinent question is no. According to the regulations they get unequal treatment.
A person from Chile on the run from a bloody dictator may be rejected. Some of them are rejected by Canadians on the grounds alleged by Canadian Government representatives that they cannot prove satisfactorily that they have a well founded fear of persecution if they stay in Chile or return to Chile.
However, persons who come from Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, German Democratic Republic, Hungary,
Poland, Romania, U.S.S.R. or Yugoslavia, according to the government's self exiled person class regulations, are not examined on that point at all. It simply states that they will be considered if they are citizens, former citizens or former residents of a country listed in Schedule 1 and are outside of Canada and are not residing or sojourning in any of the countries listed in Schedules 1 or 2, including those countries I mentioned, and are unwilling or unable to return to their country of citizenship or former habitual residence. It does not say anything about a well founded fear of persecution. The regulation goes on to state that they will be considered if they have not become permanently resettled and are seeking resettlement in Canada. There is a double standard, and it works against refugees from most countries in the world.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
According to Government policy, as I am sure was true under past Liberal governments as well, a person from Chile who is applying for refugee status faces an extra obstacle before achieving refugee status in this country. They must establish a well founded fear of political prosecution, of death or other persecution in that country. Is that what my colleague is saying?
How could anyone doubt that someone from a country like Chile does not have a well founded fear? Anyone who visits Chile would have no doubt that the people in Chile live in terror. One only need walk the streets of Santiago to feel the fear and terror under which people live. It is the very essence of that political system.
How could a Canadian Government official ever doubt that a person who has been politically active in Chile would not have a well founded fear? Unless someone is a special assistant to General Pinochet, the very nature of the political system in Chile would provide a basis for someone to have a well founded fear.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I cannot say what is in the minds of Government officials in terms of doubt. I can say what the action was in one typical case. Chileans who were flying to Canada to claim refugee status stopped en route at Buenos Aires. A Canadian consular official went on board and before even talking to them said they were not refugees, just economic migrants. When a reputable Canadian lawyer, an expert in refugee affairs, was sent at private expense to Buenos Aires to examine them, he found a person who had been more than once imprisoned and tortured by the Chilean police for his trade union activities. Yet the Canadian official said he was not a refugee, just an economic migrant. She did not even listen to his story. That is the treatment often, but not always accorded to Chileans but not to people from Schedules 1 and 2 countries in eastern Europe.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, normally one is pleased to speak to a particular Bill. However, I think it is a disgrace that we are here, still dealing with this Bill, on the anniversary of the arrival of 147 Sikhs on Canadian shores. We were called back to the House of Commons on the pretext of a crisis in Which we needed immediate laws to
July 12, 1988

handle this supposed untenable situation. We were presented with this Draconian legislation.
The fourth Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) appears to be more flexible. She obviously understands what needs to be done. I agree with her that we require proper laws in this land. We knew that in 1983 when we asked Rabbi Plaut to chair a committee that would give us an indication of how to deal with refugees who come here. We wanted to be a safe harbour to those in need and legitimately had the right to claim that status here. We wanted the kind of security measures and assurances to monitor and ensure that unworthy and unwanted people coming to this shore would not be given safe harbour. Yet neither problem has been answered adequately by a Government that does not seem to understand how to draft a Bill that reflects the Canadian attitude of openness toward strangers in need. Those who have no right to be in this land are not welcome.
The Minister is right in saying that we must send a message that undesirables are not welcome in Canada. Furthermore, those who confuse the issue by lying and stealing from those who would come here must be dealt with as well. Adequate punishments must be imposed.
The Draconian legislation introduced by the Government is before us once again on the anniversary of the arrival of the Sikhs. The Senate proposed some very intelligent and rational changes. It really was the Chamber of sober second thought. It was all Senators, not just Liberal Senators, who made recommendations. They strongly suggested there were errors made in this Bill both with respect to the methodology of turning back the boats and in the way it was written around the aiding and abetting of church groups and private citizens who, in a sense, were acting like good solid Canadians in lending the kind of help that I think the Minister intended in principle be acknowledged. However, the Bill unforgivably ignored the basic principles suggested by the Senate.
Let us look at how these things were ignored and how the Senate was rejected with respect to the compromises it put forward. Let me say in entre parentheses that I come from a riding in which almost 40 per cent of its membership have come to Canada in the last 30 years. They have built the fabric of the Mount Royal riding into an absolutely exciting and dynamic multicultural, cosmopolitan part of the City of Montreal, of Canada and of Quebec. I have talked to the Sikhs and to the Vietnamese boat people who have built up a wonderful centre in this riding.
If we had had this kind of narrow-minded mentality 20 years ago, we would not be enriched by those people and the kind of economy and personal initiative they have brought to this country, and that goes for the whole Caribbean Diaspora where there are problems, as you well know, Madam Speaker. It goes for the Tamils as well and I think the Minister should come to my riding and talk to these people. She would then
Immigration Act, 1976
correct the errors in this Bill. She would not turn back boats with these conditions and she would not charge as aiding and abetting with fines and imprisonment for people who have had some disagreement with Bill C-55.
The fundamental prescreening process is in some disagreement. The safe third country concept is an unacceptable concept because there is no real way of ensuring a safe third country. There is an inadequate non-universal appeal system which goes to the Federal Court, a court which does not have the kind of training or expertise that is required to examine a refugee claimant in order to determine their status in an intelligent and enlightened way. These are human beings. These are people who have families, who have children and whose lives are in danger. So there is a disagreement on the fundamental process.
These church groups, public advocacy groups, and fundamentally well-intentioned people are there to look at the individual cases to see if they can help them get the proper documentation. When the Senate wanted to protect those who acted in that way in a more open and upfront non-clandestine way, we say no. These are good solid Canadians of good will and we make them cheat. That is ridiculous. That is where we have to make some changes.
There are lawyers who want to help real refugees who are seeking the kinds of information a refugee needs. A refugee cannot stop and run back to his country because he needs his papers. He is fleeing a country which is no longer home to him. Anyone who has had to move from one city to another knows the trauma of dislocation and relocation, language, culture, environment, weather, the whole bit. These kindly and concerned lawyers try to enable a refugee to get their proper documentation but they will be harassed and subject to fines, and unnecessarily so. It is too bad that that was not changed.
I listened to the Minister as she talked about the refugees who were to be excluded from the refugee determination processing system and that she alone is responsible for that final decision. I think the Minister takes a terrible chance with those kinds of responsibilities. One should not disallow in that way for security purposes, but I know she has already said no to that amendment. It boggles my mind that she has said no to so many sound and intelligent amendments.
With respect to the deterrence and punishment procedure of people who are already on boats, my colleague, ho, I would suggest, has given a carefully listening ear to people who have experienced this refugee system. He has travelled and has heard from people who have experienced this particular trauma of dislocation. He has brought to our attention a very credible amendment which I would like to support very strongly. Under Section 91.1 the Minister may make a direction if she is satisfied that the vehicle can return to its port of embarkation without endangering the lives of its passengers. That is utterly ridiculous. Is she going to get frogmen out to take a look at the underside of the boat to see if it is safe? Is she going to investigate inside the boat?

July 12, 1988
There are four conditions here. If the vehicle is 12 to 24 miles outside of our country, it would have to be determined and then decided whether or not to send the passengers back to their country of origin, if they have refugee status, if they are nationals or if they are citizens of that country. The whole thing is just a mess of potash and I would suggest it be returned and looked at again. She should instead bring in the ship, arrest the captain, throw the book at him, throw the key away, and impound the ship. That is the kind of message we should be sending out to the world. We should be saying: "If you bring your boat in here, mister, you will end up in jail and you, the owner of the boat, say goodbye to your property". Believe me, they would not then be involved in this kind of illicit action such as bringing in illegitimate refugees, because we do not want those illegitimate refugees. We want productive, hard working, honourable people. Those are the kind of refugees who are welcome in this country.
I would like to speak about Section 91.1(1), where the Minister believes on reasonable grounds that a vehicle within the internal waters of Canada or the territorial sea of Canada is bringing any person into Canada in contravention of this Act or the regulation, the Minister may direct that the vehicle be escorted to the nearest port. Why "may"? It should read the Minister shall be obliged to. That is what Canadians want. It should read, after the boat has been escorted to the port of disembarkation and any such direction "shall" be enforced by such force as is reasonably necessary. In that way the search and the seizure could be done, the bona fides of the refugees involved could be established and the captain could be taken from the boat as well. I hope there will be serious consideration and support in this House for the amendments put forward by my colleague.
