subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) does not appeal to or speak for rational Canadians when he says that Canadians are tired of the trade debate and just want to see the deal approved because they have made up their minds.
Does he not realize that the latest polls show more Canadians oppose than support the deal?
The Minister for International Trade does not appeal to the pride and independence of Canadians when he says that the trade legislation cannot be changed by Parliament. Why should Canadians bother to elect Members of Parliament if they are to sit impotent and approve a Bill which overrides all other federal or provincial legislation that conflicts with the agreement?
The Minister for International Trade underestimates how much Canadians value water when he treats casually Illinois Governor Thompson's demand to triple the flow of water from Lake Michigan to the Midwest rivers.
When will the Minister for International Trade come to his
senses?

subsubtopic: RANGE FIRES CAUSED BY LOCOMOTIVE SPARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ranchers in southwestern Saskatchewan are understandably upset over the numerous range fires caused by sparks from locomotives along the right of way of the Canadian Pacific Railway main line. These fires spread rapidly, causing considerable damage to the grassland. As well, the time and effort of countless numbers of local residents, neighbours, and volunteers are expended on the containment of these fires.
The ranchers question whether the spark arresters on the locomotives are properly maintained. They also ask why the CPR does not conduct more controlled burnings of the right of way in order to reduce the fire hazard. Finally, they ask why they should be fighting the CPR's fires thereby placing themselves at risk, without compensation.
Feelings in the southwest are running high. Some ranchers indicate they are prepared to burn the right of way themselves if the CPR will not do so.
In short, residents along the main line of the CPR resent the cavalier attitude of the railway. They ask that action be taken in order to maintain properly the right of way and the spark arresters on the locomotives.

subsubtopic: RETURN OF CARMEN QUINTANA TO CHILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening a young woman of uncommon courage

July 12, 1988

and grace is going home. Despite the obscene efforts of a wicked military regime to dismember her body and still her voice, Carmen Quintana is returning to Chile, determined, as always, to serve the cause of justice and democracy.
With the help and support of countless friends in Chile and Canada, caring burn doctors and nurses, she has defied medical odds, and General Pinochet. Tonight, she will do as she always vowed she would-return to her troubled homeland.
For the Chilean people she is living testimony that the human spirit endures and, ultimately, conquers the practitioners of terror. "I want to work with the Chilean people to bring back democracy", Carmen said yesterday as she bid us goodbye.
Albert Camus once wrote: "Those who love and are separated can live in suffering, but not in despair; they know love exists".
Carmen Quintana is returning to a land she loves. She is returning to a people she loves. She goes home with the love and admiration of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: RETURN OF CARMEN QUINTANA TO CHILE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND JAMES BAY CREE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a 14 million dollar agreement was announced today by the Government of Canada and the James Bay Cree; this is a first step in the freeing up of negotiations on the implementation of the James Bay Convention with the Cree.
The agreement marks the end of a dispute revolving around four years' worth of adjustments to the amount of transfer payments to be made to the Cree for part of municipal service charges, that is the operating expenses of local and regional Cree governments, fire-fighting services, public health, roads and the maintenance of public facilities and buildings.
Mr. Speaker, the accomplishments of the James Bay Cree in administering their own affairs constitute a remarkable success for the Cree and for all Canadians.
We should appreciate the work done by Big Chief Matthew Cooncome, as well as by the eight Chiefs from Cree villages, Judge Rejean Paul, federal negotiator Andrew Croll and Roderick Pachano, the Cree's negotiator. Mr. Pachano stated that the permanent relation between the Cree government and the Canadian government is based on respect for the spirit of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Convention. In the absence of goodwill, it is hard to accomplish anything at all.
Today's agreement marks the beginning of the reinstatement of trust.

Mr. Speaker, we are a few weeks or a few days away from an election call and the Conservative government, after four years, still has not settled 12 priority issues important for Quebec: the Space Agency; the Banking Center; the development of the Port of Montreal; the improvements to the Old Port of Montreal; the contract for the construction of railway engines for Bombardier; the CN maintenance shops in southwest Montreal; the paper mill in Matane; a bridge on route 30 for the City of Valleyfield; a specific agriculture policy for Quebec; early retirement, and the Lauzon, Sorel and Montreal shipyards.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude with that. This is what we are wondering about at the present time: is the Government delaying its decisions in order to announce them during the election campaign in the hope that Quebecers will forget its incompetence and its neglect of them over the past four years? Or does it simply not have the courage to make decisions because there is disagreement within its caucus about the Space Agency?

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) recently announced that Canadians who served in the Korean War are being awarded Korean Service Badges by Canada for the first time in 35 years.
On July 26 we will celebrate the thirty-fifth anniversary of the end of the Korean War. As we commemorate that day, we can be proud that it was this Government that at long last has seen fit to show Canada's appreciation for the dedication and sacrifice of Canadian servicemen who fought for freedom in that conflict.
Up until the recent announcement by the Minister, Korean War veterans were awarded British service medals and United Nations service medals only, and unlike veterans who served in the First and Second World Wars received no specific recognition from their own country.

The Korean Service Badges recognize the contribution made by veterans who served with the Canadian Forces or associated support groups between June 27, 1950, and July 27, 1954. The Minister also announced that the immediate family of a deceased veteran may apply for the badge.
It is about time that these brave men and women received an official thank you from the people and Government of Canada, and I dm very proud to be a member of the Government that has finally made this possible.

Mr. Speaker, I have been privileged to live in the nation's capital for nearly three decades. I describe this national capital as a jewel, even though every jewel needs a little polishing. This capital possesses great natural beauty. It is a safe and secure place in which to live, work, and raise a family. It has great schools, universities, research and cultural institutions.
The National Capital Commission recently prepared a discussion paper entitled "The Capital Orientation Plan". The NCC has a mandate to ensure that our capital serves as a meeting place, bringing Canadians together through the democratic process; communicating Canada to Canadians; and safeguarding and preserving those national treasures which are unique in their influence on all Canadians- in short, the mandate to turn our capital into a national symbol.
One of the Commission's principal proposals is to make known the major achievements of Canadians. This could be done by creating a Canadian Hall of Fame in the capital which would recognize both individual and collective achievements and contributions to the quality of Canadian life. I would like to encourage the National Capital Commission in achieving its goals.

Mr. Speaker, as communications critic for the New Democratic Party, I am concerned about the lock-out by CFTO-TV in Toronto. It looks like the company is simply out to break the union and it is clearly bargaining in bad faith in order to do so.
I quote from someone who is not what I would consider a leftie, and that is Lorrie Goldstein of the Toronto Sun. He said:
July 12, 1988
Personally, I don't like unions.
Having said that, if CFTO-TV chief Doug Bassett was my boss, I'd probably be a union man.
I am concerned especially about their biased news reporting of their own strike. That is an abuse of the freedom of the press, abuse of the airwaves, and the CRTC should look into that. I am also concerned that cabinet Ministers have been crossing the picket lines in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) says that he would never cross picket lines and cabinet Ministers are not supposed to do so.
This is a mean, vicious strike. The management of CFTO better realize that there are larger issues involved here and get a settlement of the lock-out strike.

subsubtopic: BEIRUT REFUGEE CAMPS-ARMED STRUGGLE FOR CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again innocent men, women, and children in the Beirut refugee camps of Shatila and Bourj-el-Barajneh have been caught up in the crossfire of rival PLO militia groups who have been struggling for control.
Since the beginning of May approximately 170 people have been killed and over 600 wounded as a result of the fighting between the mainstream PLO Fatah forces of Yasser Arafat and those of his Syrian-sponsored rival, Col. Said Mussa's Fatah-Uprising faction. Witnesses say that "virtually every building in the Shatila camp has been wrecked or severely damaged". PLO officials state that 80 per cent of the Bourj-el-Barajneh camp has been destroyed by bombardments over the last 60 days.
On June 27, Mr. Arafat's group was forced to surrender the Shatila camp to Mr. Mussa's men after losing a three-month battle that killed over 90 people. While this brought the fighting in that camp to an end, a number of Fatah fighters requested and were granted safe passage by Libyan mediators to Mr. Arafat's bases near Sidon. There they will undoubtedly regroup to fight other battles and claim more innocent lives. By July 7 the Bourj-el-Barajneh camp had fallen to Mr. Mussa's forces, with 38 people being killed and 93 wounded since the battle for the camp intensified on July 4.
There has been no official Canadian government statement about this slaughter. It is unbelievably strange that such scant media attention has been given this brutal tragedy which has lasted several months. Canada should give consideration to what measures it can take to help innocent people escape the factional warfare of the PLO that inevitably leads to the death of their own refugees.
July 12, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the people of Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup are delighted with the adoption on third reading of Bill C-72, the Official Languages Bill.
I wanted to raise the subject today and express my unqualified appreciation of our democratic system, thanks to which the equality of French and English as official languages within our federal institutions has finally been recognized.
Mr. Speaker, the passage of this Bill has corrected a situation that in this day and age was becoming intolerable. In fact, it took a Conservative Government and our Conservative Prime Minister, who has the courage of his convictions, to table and adopt the Official Languages Act, something the Liberal Government under Pierre Elliott Trudeau was afraid to do.
Mr. Speaker, the democratic process has dealt with certain individuals in this country who had a narrow and unbending attitude towards the French fact. Personally, I believe that our diversity and our respect for our differences will enhance our stature as a nation.

subsubtopic: WESTERN DROUGHT-ASSISTANCE SOUGHT BY BRITISH COLUMBIA BEEF PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the South Kamloops Stockmen's Association recently informed the Minister of Agriculture for Canada (Mr, Wise) about the very critical situation its members are facing as a result of the prolonged, hot and dry weather. With herds representing thousands of head of cattle, their present water supplies are completely inadequate, and many ranchers are forced to haul water. Some have been hauling water since last fall and some ranchers presently have no water supply at all.
The situation looks especially bleak for this fall, and it means that there will likely be no water at all for this winter. The drought in the Thompson-Nicola region of British Columbia is at a crisis stage and these beef producers require immediate and special assistance.
I urge the Minister of Agriculture to take action immediately to provide the members of the South Kamloops Stockmen's Association with a subsidy to offset their recent drought related costs so that they will not be forced to sell off their herds.
These cattlemen form a crucial component of our regional economy and all efforts must be made to ensure their survival during these extremely dry months.
When we think of western agriculture, Mr. Speaker, often our thinking stops at the Rockies. I urge the Minister of Agriculture to remember all those struggling through the drought, including those ranchers in the interior valleys of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business is seeking protection from unfair financial service charges on small businesses. It says that a measure of justice has already been accorded to the consumers of Canada, but much more is needed to be granted to small business people affected by financial institutions.
Particularly the Federation asks that financial institutions provide complete information on changes when they are to be made to service charges. It wants charge-back fees on NSF cheques eliminated. It calls for an annual monitoring of service charges as they apply to small businesses, and it seeks an appeal process to redress grievances.
The Government has already made a beginning in responding to these recommendations. I urge it to finish the job. The health of small business is vital to Canada's economy. We are aware that the key problem in this instance is the extreme imbalance of power between the Financial institutions and small businesses. Here is an opportunity for Parliament and the Government to provide the equalizer.

subsubtopic: DISBANDMENT OF NEWFOUNDLAND RAILWAY-EFFECT ON NORTH SYDNEY, N.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the Government on June 20 announced the closure of the Newfoundland Railway it said that the town of North Sydney would not be affected. Yet on the same day the President of CN said that he was starting a new boat service from Halifax to St. John's. The very next day, CN sent a directive to all its outlets saying that as of June 25 all containers in eastern Newfoundland, east of Gander, would be shipped from Halifax to St. John's.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO-EFFECT OF PROVINCIAL POLICIES ON HEALTH SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Peterson Government has announced that 101 beds at Wellesly Elospital must remain closed in order to meet budgetary restraints. In fact the Peterson Government will soon force more bed closures in all hospitals across the province as a result of its overspending in other fields. What hypocrisy!
What happened to the 1987 election promise of $3 billion toward health care? The Peterson Government recently enacted one of the biggest tax grabs in Ontario history by raising taxes across the board, including substantial hikes in sales and personal income taxes. Yet the Peterson Government is ignoring health care, the most vital of all government services. It is apparent that the Government of Ontario places politics above the health of its citizens.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. Last night, our deputy chief trade negotiator, Ambassador Gordon Ritchie, declared for the first time that during the talks with the United States, Canadian experts from the Department of the Environment and experts on our negotiating team had drafted a special clause to exclude, to exempt our water from the FTA, and that the Canadian negotiating team had never insisted on getting this exemption.
Mr. Speaker, this raises some troubling questions. First of all, why have Conservative ministers systematically denied before the House that there had ever been any intention of excluding water? Why this misleading attitude? And second, since the trade legislation has paramountcy over Canada's water policy, why didn't Canada insist on obtaining this exclusion which was judged to be necessary by our experts from the Department of the Environment?
Mr. Speaker, it seems very difficult for the Leader of the Opposition to understand that water was never on the table in the free trade negotiations.
Hear, hear!
Quite frankly, the Leader of the Opposition may not want to understand that because, of course, his past references to water would lead us to believe that he indeed would have put it on the table.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: He would have given it away.

There is no question about where this Government stands on the issue of large-scale diversions of water. We have said that there will be no large-scale diversion of water from this country. What is more, we have done something which the Liberal Party had never done in all its time in office. We have issued a water policy which expressly prohibits the exportation and the diversion of large-scale amounts of water.
I think it is about time that the Leader of the Opposition understood what this issue is all about, without trying to contrive some false approach which simply does not hold water.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I had known for a long time the Minister was Acting Prime Minister today, but I regret to say that she appears to have caught the contagious bombastic disease of her absent seat-mate. We might as well have been listening to the Minister for International Trade today. His philosophy when dealing with the House of Commons is simple.
Deny, deny, deny.
No, it is don't read the deal. That is number one. Don't debate the issues. That is number two. Try to bluff your way out of any falsehood you can. That is number three.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Acting Prime Minister, while she is in
July 12, 1988

such a benign mood, on such a complex, serious and vital issue for Canada as this, why are Canadians being allowed less than one month to come to Ottawa to appear before the committee and to express their views on this crucial trade arrangement with the United States? Why do the residents of Vancouver Quadra, or of any other riding in Canada, have to travel hundreds or thousands of miles to come to Ottawa to get the chance to have their say on this Bill? Why is the Government afraid of the Canadian public?

Mr. Speaker, once again the Leader of the Opposition expresses his own fears. If there is one individual in one Party who is afraid of the Canadian public, he is sitting opposite in this House of Commons.
The free trade debate has gone on for a long period of time. It has been debated. It has been raised by hundreds of organizations and thousands of individuals across the country.
Obviously there will be presentations put to the parliamentary committee within the next month. I would think that the individual Members of Parliament who sit on that committee will give very proper attention to those who come before them. There will be full and adequate hearings, and the members of the committee will give proper consideration to the presentations that are made.

Mr. Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister has a unique opportunity. She is in charge today of the Government of Canada. She can leave the House immediately, go see the Governor General, and let's issue the writ. What about that?
Go, go!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister has been briefed by the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown. He is looking real tough there. He had better get back to his constituency and protect his behind.
Oh, oh!

The Acting Prime Minister talked about fear. More than a month ago the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister of Canada, Mr. Burney, in a panic, flew down to Washington because, on behalf of the Government of Canada, he was disturbed about what might be in the American legislation, particularly having to do with the tribunal and with the definition of subsidy.
My question is this. How can the parliamentary committee studying the Canadian legislation implementing the deal have any confidence that Canadian concerns expressed by the Prime Minister's Office about the American legislation have been addressed when that legislation has not yet been made public?
Oral Questions
What is the idea of the Government pushing our legislation through this House in such a hurry when we have not yet seen the American legislation? Why the obscene haste?

Two points with regard to the preamble, Mr. Speaker. One has to do with recent elections. The Lac-Saint-Jean result would not, I think, provide any great support or encouragement to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition.
Hear, hear!
Second, because he raised the issue-
You bought that election.
Now we are hearing from the NDP which managed 9 per cent of the vote in Lac-Saint-Jean.
Oh, oh!

The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition raised another point when he said that Mr. Burney went down to Washington in a panic. I want to assure him that I have never known Mr. Burney to do anything in a panic.
Finally, I want to say that we are proceeding with legislation in this House and in committee because this happens to be a sovereign Parliament. We decide the process and the way this Parliament will implement legislation in this country. We do not, like the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition seems to think, take direction from the people he listens to in Washington. Those are the ways in which the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition seems to think this Parliament should operate. We do not think that way because we know this is a sovereign Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I can only say to the Acting Prime Minister that if her assessment of the key to electoral success for the Tory Party in Lac-Saint-Jean was $164 million, it will cost the Canadian people $45 billion for it to win the general election.
Write the cheque, Mike.
It would take that much to win Rosedale alone.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct this question to the Acting Prime Minister. We have seen a suppression of the rights of Parliament in its ability to provide access to Canadians to proper committee hearings and the ability to make amendments. In addition, the Canadian people are being put at a major disadvantage vis-a-vis the U.S.
The omnibus Trade Bill is now in front of Congress ready to be passed. Our senior trade negotiator, Mr. Ritchie, has acknowledged that Bill would totally undermine the trade

July 12, 1988
Oral Questions
agreement. We have the Chairman of the Finance Committee saying that the U.S. Congress will introduce major new subsidy requirements for Canada as part of its implementing legislation. We now have two damaging pieces of trade legislation before the U.S. Congress, yet we are going to rush our Bill through without proper hearings.
Do you have a question sometime this afternoon?

Why is the Government ready to suppress the rights of this Parliament and put Canadians at a major disadvantage vis-a-vis the U.S. and its trade legislation, rather than taking the prudent, responsible course and ensuring that the two pieces of legislation are at least brought forward at the same time so we can see where the advantages and disadvantages lie?

Mr. Speaker, I come back to the point I raised before. Obviously the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry does not believe that this is a sovereign Parliament. We do. We feel that we should be taking the steps which we as a Government and as a legislature believe should be taken for this country.
There can always be some question as to how many Canadians are in favour of the free trade deal and how many are not. However, every survey which has been taken shows that more Canadians want to have the free trade agreement implemented than are opposed to it.
That happens to be the case with the Opposition, Once again they are backing a losing proposition. They want to tear up the free trade deal. Canadians want to see it implemented and we are doing that.

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister is saying that the Government's decision is dictated by the polls, then I point out a very important poll which appeared last week which indicated that 65 per cent of Canadians want an election on this issue. We can only conclude that the Government is afraid to have one because it is afraid to put the deal in front of the Canadian people. That happens to be the case.

Mr. Speaker, the Department of Energy of the Province of Manitoba released a study yesterday which pointed out that if the Canada-U.S. trade deal had been in effect during the last energy crisis, from 1979 to 1982, it would have cost Canadian consumers an additional $72.6 billion because we would not have been able to provide the support and protection to Canadian consumers which was available at that time.
Has the Government undertaken similar studies which would confirm these findings? Would it table those studies? Would it be able to tell us what the cost would be to Canadian
consumers if they faced another energy crisis under the Canada-U.S. trade deal? Would it be another $72.6 billion?

Mr. Speaker, I know the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry likes to pose hypothetical questions to the House-"if it should be this", "if it should be that", and so on.
Quite frankly, with regard to energy deals we saw exactly what it cost the people of Canada in the early 1980s, particularly the people of western Canada, when the former Liberal Government implemented an energy package which did immense damage to this country economically.
We are dealing with the reality of the situation rather than with hypothetical issues. We knew that the national energy plan had to be turned around and we know that this one has to go ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister as well. On June 16 the Minister for International Trade said, "Water is not affected by the free trade agreement".
Last night in committee Ambassador Ritchie indicated that "there was technical work done" on the question of exempting water from this trade deal. In fact, he indicated that there was a "technical proposition" on the matter prepared, and confirmed "some official from another Department had indicated with great pride that he had some involvement..." in that work.
Given this, why has the Government consistently maintained that there was no connection between water and the trade deal when this preparatory work had been done according to the testimony of our ambassador?

Mr. Speaker, I reiterate once again that water and the diversion of water was never on the table. I will repeat that for the Member. Water was never on the table. I hope he will understand that.
In fact, with regard to water policy we have introduced for the first time a water policy which states very clearly that there shall be no diversion of large scale water projects in this country.
I would also like to point out that Mr. Ritchie did say last night that there is nothing in the agreement which would constrain the Government in implementing its water policy. In other words, legislation dealing with water policy could flow from the statements and the policies that have already been introduced, but they are not part of the free trade agreement.

REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ON WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point, of course, is that that is precisely what Ambassador
July 12, 1988

Ritchie went on to say. He went on to say that there was nothing which would prevent action being taken to prevent such inter-basin water transfers as are now threatening the Great Lakes.
Given that there was nothing within the agreement which would prevent that, which is precisely what he said, would the Government, on an emergency basis, bring in legislation to prevent such water transfers which will damage people right across the Great Lakes basin?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ON WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two points to make. Last night Ambassador Ritchie said that water for export on a large scale was never considered to be part of the free trade agreement.
Second, I will be glad to send the Member a copy of this document dated November 5, 1987, which says, "Large-scale water diversions to the United States will not be considered by the Canadian Government under any circumstances according to the federal water policy tabled today by the Environment Minister".
I would ask the Member to read this so that he will know what the policy of the country and the Government is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ON WATER RESOURCES
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor but I think the Chair should observe that the last question was, at least in the opinion of the Chair, hypothetical. Members who are asking questions to remember the rule that hypothetical questions are, strictly speaking, out of order. I know the Hon. Member will be able to pose his question adequately.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to point out to the Acting Prime Minister that in the comments which she quoted from Ambassador Ritchie he went on to say that it may have been in error that they made that conclusion. Therefore, I ask the Minister-

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ON EMERGENCY BASIS
speechtext: Come on, be honest.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION ON EMERGENCY BASIS
speechtext:
I quote from the transcript of the committee. If the Acting Prime Minister has the transcript, let her quote it back.
Given the fact that the Government can move to put legislation in place to protect the Great Lakes basin, will the Government, on an emergency basis, bring such legislation in at once?

-which limit Members on all sides the right to ask questions.

By and large dirty words are out and during the recent past no Members have been thrown out for unparliamentary behaviour. I know of too many cases, which I will not cite here, of lengthy preambles which are irrelevant and argumentative. These diatribes-cum-political statements are being smuggled in. Some Members are speaking for too long and other Members are suffering the penalty of the clock running out at the 45-minute mark. Moreover, these violations of rules are annoying to the public because once Your Honour rises to intervene, those watching hear only the barracking, name-calling, and general schoolroom hubbub which does nothing to enhance the dignity of this place.
I realize, Sir, that the lengthy partisan pitches put you as Speaker in a difficult position. A Minister will naturally move in and take on the argumentative nature of the preamble before he or she gets to the substance of the question, and that is only fair.
But we are also having constant repetition because when one opposition Party happens to pre-empt a second opposition Party on a question, then the question is asked not once, not twice, but five times or ten times to try to get different answers and to try to make the national news. When constantly repetitive questions are asked again we are in clear violation of the rules under Beauchesne's.
Mis. Copps: We never get any answers and we will continue to ask the questions.
Mir. Scott (Hamilton-Wentworth): If the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) will quieten down for a moment more, I can remember former Liberal Government appointed Speakers and I think particularly of the Hon. Lucien Lamoureux, and Speaker James Jerome, who were constantly admonishing Conservative and New Democratic opposition Members about repetitious questions which clearly are out of order, and detailed questions which should be placed on the Order Paper.
In conclusion, if we do not exactly need to overhaul Question Period, there are a couple of routes that we could take to restore some of the dignity and decorum of this place. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest that one route we could take would be to refer Question Period concerns to the House Leaders of the three Parties, or second, and perhaps preferable, to the House Leadership of the colleagues who have enough on their plates these days, it might be advisable to set up an ad hoc committee of concerned colleagues on all sides of the House to compile our thoughts and suggestions on tightening up Question Period.
The goal would be to allow for better exchanges and more questions, thereby making life easier on Members and on our viewing audience. Clearly we need some mechanism to resurrect the true nature of Question Period and to make more effective this most high profile hour of any sitting day.

Wentworth)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with an unusual display of crocodile tears unheard of in this Parliament, if not in the history of Parliament, whether or not he realizes it, the Hon. Member has reflected unfairly on your conduct, Sir, of Question Period. The Hon. Member has made continued reference to what he calls the "rules". There are only two references in the rules, that is, the Standing Orders of the House with respect to Question Period. One Standing Order relates to when in the day Question Period takes place, and how long it should be, and it is 45 minutes, not one hour. Second, Standing Order 65(l)(a) states:
Questions on matters of urgency may, at the time specified in Standing
Order 19(4), be addressed orally to Ministers of the Crown, provided
however that, if in the opinion of the Speaker a question is not urgent, he or
she may direct that it be placed on the Order Paper.
This has always been interpreted to mean that the Speaker has the absolute discretion as to the type of questions and, for that matter, the answers, that may be allowed during Question Period. However, from time to time individual Speakers have announced guidelines as to how they would use the power given to them under the Standing Orders with respect to Question Period. These guidelines have been published in successive editions of Beauchesne's.
My hon. friend has failed to note that the most recent set of guidelines were those announced in this Parliament by your distinguished predecessor. Those guidelines were set down some time after this Parliament began, and some time after the practices which my hon. friend appears to be complaining of were established and very much in terms of precedents as to what were accepted, not only by yourself, but your predecessors in other Parliaments.
I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that if my hon. friend is complaining about preambles, if my hon. friend is complaining about the content of questions, then in all fairness he should also talk about the answers. He should particularly talk about the length of answers and what often appears to be a deliberate effort, and I hope I am wrong in this, on the part of Ministers answering to talk out Question Period and to do the very thing my hon. friend complains of, that is, to prevent Hon. Members on both sides of the House from putting questions within the time limited by the rules for Question Period.
I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to this rather strange and unfortunate lack of balance in the point of order of my hon. friend. Everything my hon. friend complains of was done over and over again in previous Parliaments by members of his Party when they were in Opposition and therefore precedents were established in terms of preambles, in terms of length of questions, and in terms of content of questions which I do not think that my hon. friend can credibly complain of at this time because of what he and his colleagues did when they were in Opposition.
In conclusion, as far as I am concerned you have the judgment, Mr. Speaker, in the exercise of the authority given to you under our rules to deal with the matter of Question

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There are 15 motions on the Order Paper and Notices offered in amendment to Bill C-l 10, an Act to establish the Canadian International Trade Tribunal and to amend or repeal other Acts in consequence thereof.
Motions Nos. 1 to 7 inclusive, 10, 11, 13 and 14, stand in the name of the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Lang-don).
Motions Nos. 8, 12 and 15 stand in the name of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson).

The Chair has some hesitation about Motion No. 1 which adds to Clause 2 a definition of the term "domestic producers of goods". According to the definition, this term would cover any firm employing, or any trade union representing, workers producing the goods involved. If I understand the Bill correctly, the right to file a complaint directly with the International Trade Tribunal, on the grounds of injury as defined in the legislation, is granted to all Canadian producers.
Under Paragraph 26(1 )(b), an inquiry by the International Trade Tribunal into a complaint may not be initiated unless the complaint is made by or on behalf of domestic producers who produce a major proportion of domestic production of the like or directly competitive goods. There is no provision for direct access to the International Trade Tribunal by a firm employing, or any trade union representing, workers producing the goods involved.

Furthermore, the Member is attempting to take the power away from the Governor in Council to make regulations with respect to defining the term "domestic producers" in Clause 40(b).

For the reasons just mentioned, I have concluded that this amendment is beyond the scope of the Bill as adopted on second reading in the Elouse.
Furthermore, this is a substantive amendment of the interpretation clause of the Bill. I would refer the Hon. Member to citation 773 (10) of Beauchesne's, Fifth Edition, page 233, and I quote:
(10) A substantive amendment may not be introduced by way of a modification to the interpretation clause of a bill. Journals, May 21, 1970, p. 835.
Consequently, the motion is ruled out of order.

1 have concerns with regard to Motions Nos. 2, 3 and 4. These motions are related because the intent is to grant the International Trade Tribunal the power to initiate injury-related inquiries on its own. I understand that an identical motion as to Motion No. 3 was ruled out of order at the committee stage. In Clause 16, the powers, duties and functions of the International Trade Tribunal are stated. These powers are further elaborated in Clauses 18, 19 and 20 which provide for the kind of references of inquiries which the Governor in Council and the Minister of Finance may authorize the International Trade Tribunal to undertake.

According to the Chair, it would be beyond the scope of the Bill as adopted on second reading by the House to give the International Trade Tribunal the power to conduct inquiries as a matter of course. The motion is therefore ruled out of order.

It is for this reason that I have moved these amendments. They have some relationship to some other amendments about which I will be talking later. However, with respect to the various motions, if I can go through them in order, Motion No. 5 is an attempt to loosen up and perhaps clarify also for companies the information which they have to provide to this new Canadian international trade tribunal in order to have a hearing in front of that tribunal. An industry is asked to provide certain information and the information for this complaint, as in the present Clause 22, left it very much to the tribunal to decide if it is satisfied that it has been presented with the material required by Clause 22.
My amendment to the motion suggests that it is not up to the tribunal to make this decision but simply that if the details which are outlined in Clause 23 are in fact provided to the tribunal, then the complaint must be heard. In short, it opens up access to the tribunal itself so that our industries across the country, which are affected by import pressure, can put their complaints before this tribunal successfully.
With respect to Motion No. 6, what we are attempting to do is to set forth a somewhat looser definition of what constitutes import pressure or import damage. The key point in comparing the two clauses, the existing Clause 23 and the suggested amendment, is that we have to take account, in analysing what import damage is, not just of the quantities and the conditions which might cause or threaten serious injury to domestic producers, but the prices at which these imports are coming into the country. If these prices are, for instance, such as to themselves constitute a threat which could cost us thousands of jobs, even if there has been no change in the quantities or in the basic competitive conditions which exist within the industry, the difference which is constituted by such prices is something which should be taken into account by the tribunal.
I should indicate that a number of these amendments have been directly influenced by the testimony put before our trade tribunal hearings on Bill C-110 by the various witnesses who made presentations from industry, from the existing textile and clothing board chairperson and from certain testimony written and provided by trade unions.
With respect to Motion No. 7, the suggestion here refers to Clause 26. Again there is an attempt to introduce into Clause
Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act
26 this same notion of prices as an important consideration in considering the potential impact of imports coming into the country. I think, if I may say so, that to ignore the price at which imports are coming into the country is really a serious gap in this present Bill.
With respect to the other motion which is grouped here, which is Motion No. 10, precisely the same point is being made with respect to Clause 27. Clause No. 27 in this case also leaves out the question of price.
As economists would want to point out, price and the potential undercutting of price which exists with respect to those items which are produced here in Canada are important considerations. One really cannot determine what is supposed to be determined by each of these clauses, which is the potential to cause or threaten to cause serious or other injury to domestic production of like or directly competitive goods.
If I can conclude, Madam Speaker, these are minor amendments but ones which I believe will improve significantly this Bill with respect to the benefits which Canadian industry may expect to receive from the Bill in the future.

Madam Speaker, I would like to respond to my hon. friend's proposed amendments to this Bill. I commend him for the close interest he has taken in this piece of legislation. I have to disagree with him when he says that these are minor amendments. In fact, they add up to a major attack on the whole concept of the GATT. His Party has often suggested that the GATT be appealed to in the place of, for example, the free trade agreement. In this particular set of amendments, and in others which I think he will propose later, he is attacking in essence fundamental standards behind the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. I want to address myself to those amendments in order to make this clear to the House.
I would also like to say that there may be a misunderstanding in his close study of the Bill in terms of the wider context in which this Bill is placed. He began his comments-and this may be the source of his troubles-with reference to some of the powers that the present Textile and Clothing Board has, in particular its authority to self-initiate an inquiry about injury. I remind the Hon. Member that the Textile and Clothing Board has only used this authority in the past to self-initiate an inquiry about injury in the context of reviews of existing textile and clothing import quotas to determine whether or not they should be continued or varied. One would have to be pretty conversant with the board to know that. But that in fact has been the history.
Inquiries into new product areas, something which may be at the heart of the Hon. Member's concern, which can be initiated at the request of industry or the Minister, are different. The provisions of this Bill, Bill C-110, will continue to let industry petition the tribunal for inquiries into new product areas or to let the Government request an inquiry.

July 12, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act
That is not being blocked. There is no power that the Textile and Clothing Board has today that would not be available with regard to new product areas under Bill C-110 for the new trade tribunal that we are establishing.
I think the Hon. Member is concerned about where the restraints come from to prevent us from having a flood of imports, textiles and so on into Canada. That is part of the broader context, too, that I want to point out to him. These broader restraints imposed on textile and clothing imports into Canada come from the negotiation of bilateral agreements with exporting countries under the multi-fibre arrangement. This arrangement, known as the MFA, which is a derogation from the GATT in that it provides for border actions on the basis of bilateral agreements rather than on a global basis against imports from all sources, is still in place. I made that point in committee. However, I do not know whether or not the Hon. Member was there that day. Nothing will change that. The MFA only requires evidence that textile and clothing imports are causing what is called market disruption. No compensation is required to be paid when these arrangements are worked out.
In comparison, a safeguard action, which is what we are talking about this afternoon, is totally different. So that whole process, the non-safeguard part of the textile and clothing arrangement, those bilateral agreements under the MFA, remain. It is business as usual for them.
During the past 10 years, and more particularly since 1981, the Government has used bilateral restraint agreements to protect the textile and clothing industry. These restraint agreements permitted under the multi-fibre arrangement are very flexible and much less costly than taking safeguard actions. That is not the way to deal with this matter. The way to go is to work on those bilateral restraint agreements if flexibility is wanted.
It is important for me also to tell the House that External Affairs officials are responsible for the bilateral negotiations and deals with industry problems. They deal with these problems as requests arise. It is a very flexible system. The industry is well aware of the process in that area. I gather the industry said that during the committee hearings that were held on the morning of May 19. This is a broad context to deal with all of these amendments which have been suggested.
Let me deal precisely with the motions. I gather Motions Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4, if I heard the Speaker properly, are out of order. I will speak now to Motions Nos. 5, 6, 7 and 10, which I believe are to be debated at this time.
Motion No. 5 deals with Clause 22. The basis of the Hon. Member's amendment would seriously weaken the requirement that a complaint be documented properly. As a matter of fact, if one starts to attack the concept of proper documentation, one can find the whole evidence of safeguard actions tumbling down.
I understand the desire that the Hon. Member has expressed to avoid imposing an undue information requirement on producers petitioning the new tribunal. However, for the tribunal to undertake an inquiry and to examine for serious injury it is absolutely indispensable that the tribunal be satisfied that the documentation it has before it is adequate at the outset and thus later avoid no injury findings because of inadequate initial information.
Because of the lower standard in the proposed amendment, the complaint may be deemed to be properly documented, even if the tribunal is not able to satisfy itself that the complaint contains the necessary information. This is a very awkward posture for the tribunal to be put into. However, once a complaint is accepted as properly documented the tribunal has only 30 days to decide whether or not to initiate a safeguard inquiry. In such cases the tribunal may not be able to initiate an investigation because the complaint may not have disclosed an acceptable indication of increased imports causing serious injury. Because of the documentation problem this amendment is flawed.
With respect to Motion No. 6, in essence, it would put Canada ultra vires with respect to our obligations to the GATT. The changes embodied in this proposed amendment to Clause 23 and the corresponding change to Clause 26 would put Canada ultra vires with respect to its GATT obligations for Article 19, safeguard actions. These are obligations for everybody and not just for Canada under the GATT. The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) is proposing that there be a right of direct access in the case of a threat of increased imports, whereas GATT requires an increase in imports, not a threat, not a dark cloud, but actual empirical proof that there is an increase in imports.
Aside from the amendment being inconsistent with GATT, opening up the system in this manner would have a very chilling effect on trade. If this process were used in this manner, we would cause reverberations with our trading partners. Similarly, allowing for direct access where only injury rather than serious injury has occurred would also be inconsistent with the GATT safeguard provisions. Injury is not consistent with GATT; serious injury is consistent with GATT.
The amendment of the Hon. Member makes its case on injury rather than on serious injury. The Hon. Member may be attempting to alter the basic purpose of the legislation to allow the tribunal to undertake direct access inquiries for nonsafeguard purposes. That may be what the Hon. Member's attempt is. However, the legislation is not designed for nonsafeguard purposes. It is there for the whole safeguard process. That amendment is a serious mistake.
I now want to speak to Motion No. 7 which speaks to Clause 26. It is the same problem, and I already spelled out my concerns with this motion when I addressed the amendment proposed to Clause 23 in Motion No. 6. GATT does not permit
July 12, 1988

Article 19 safeguard action on the basis of a threat of imports, or on the basis of any other type of injury funding other than "serious injury". Therefore, there has to be serious injury to put this process in place under Article 19 of GATT. My argument for Motion No. 7 is the same as my argument for Motion No. 6.
Finally, Motion No. 10 speaks to Clause 27. The amendment proposed in Motion No. 10 to Clause 27 would radically change the concept of the legislation in its entirety. This clause was discussed at great length in committee. The committee endorsed the concept that increased imports must be the principal cause of serious injury. The amendment set out in Motion No. 10 eliminates this concept, and at the same time introduces the notion of other injury. This is contrary to Article 19 of the GATT provisions which only provide for safeguard injury in the case of serious injury. The revised language also contains the concept of threat of imports which, as I have already stated, is not permitted under GATT.
I commend the Hon. Member for following this Bill carefully, but for those reasons the amendments are not minor. They are quite major mistakes, and I say that the House must not support those amendments.

Madam Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Motion No. 8. Essentially, the Bill proposes to allow groups of domestic producers who are responsible for or represent an important part or the major proportion of a given production to file a complaint with the Tribunal asking it to conduct an inquiry to determine whether or not they have been the victims of an injustice.
The amendment I am moving on behalf of my colleague the Member for Trinity (Ms. Nicholson) is to the effect that a producer who feels that certain circumstances have caused him injury could himself file a complaint with the Tribunal to ask it to conduct an inquiry to determine whether or not Canadian

July 12, 1988

industry has been adversely affected by massive quantities of imported goods that might suddenly flow into the country at a certain point.
Madam Speaker, when the Legislative Committee debated the Bill we broadened the clause somewhat, because the original text of the Bill used the following expression, in English: "a major proportion of domestic production". "A part or a proportion of more than 50 per cent" ... and an amendment was made to modify the clause somewhat, and to say "an important part".
But there are several types of industries in Canada where large producers may represent 55, 60, or 65 per cent of production, and very often those major producers are controlled by national interests or, quite frequently, by nonresident shareholders. And for all sorts of reasons related to international ramifications, those large producers might object to complaints being filed with the Tribunal to ask that Tribunal to conduct an inquiry on the import of unreasonable quantities of goods or the sale of goods at unjustifiably low prices.
The result would be that domestic producers, or the smaller ones at least, would find it impossible to file their complaints with the Tribunal to ask it to investigate massive imports affecting them.
The Government claims that this would be an excessive simplification and might increase the complaints. In any case, small producers or producers representing 5, 6 or 7 per cent of a given production are often represented by associations that could make representations on their behalf to the Tribunal and file a complaint asking that an inquiry be conducted into the massive imports of goods being sold at overly competitive prices in the light of production costs in Canada.
It is nice to think that things might happen that way, but here again, there are several types of production where the number of producers is so small that the associations, even though they represent everyone, may have different objectives and perspectives, especially if one producer is totally dominant for a given product.
Thus, the purpose of the amendment is to make the inquiry process accessible to a domestic producer who feels that he has really been wronged. Pursuant to the clauses that precede clause 26, he would have to provide sufficient information to show that an inquiry is justified, but the amendment would allow a producer to file a complaint and initiate the process on his own.
The need is obvious if one looks at what has been done in other countries; I believe that in some recent cases in the United States, concerning potash particularly, the major producers were not the ones to file the complaint that was judged to be in order and that triggered the whole inquiry process which led to the result you are familiar with.
If American producers are protected in that way, I don't see why we on the Canadian side could not offer the same
possibility to a producer who feels that the survival of his business is threatened, as well as the jobs he offers to a certain number of Canadians; he should be able to benefit from the advantages of complaining to the Tribunal which could analyze the exaggerated increase in imports which might have occurred.

I would like to say why I think the motion by my colleague, the Hon. Member from Trinity (Miss Nicholson), moved by the Hon. Member from Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), is not something that makes sense. With many of our industries in this country, as all Members of this House know, we have vast numbers of extremely small producers. This is certainly the case with respect to the auto parts industry, which is prevalent in my constituency. It is certainly the case with respect to the clothing industry. I think it does make sense to insist that there be some proportion of the industry which has to bring a complaint. I have some concern about the existing level which has been established. It represents a compromise on the Government's part which it took in committee, and I am therefore pleased to live with that compromise.
With respect, however, to my motion, in attempting to assess the proportion of the industry which brings its complaint

before the tribunal, it is important that domestic production include or be considered to be production, leaving aside those firms which are, as my amendment suggests, related to exporters or importers of the like or directly competitive goods, or are themselves importers of such products.
We could certainly see a situation in this country where the great bulk of domestic producers were related to importers and would therefore have no interest in bringing a complaint before the tribunal. So, to leave out of the analysis what constitutes a major proportion of the domestic production of this particular good, it seems to me absolutely critical that we exclude those firms which are themselves associated with importers. Otherwise, we will be in a situation where true domestic producers are not going to be able to go before this tribunal to ask for safeguard or for other action.
I want to make a point with respect to this entire section which deals with complaints by domestic producers. This section does not, through any definition or statement in the Bill itself, limit itself to safeguard actions. It may well have been the Minister's intention that it should have been limited to safeguard actions. If that is the case, there is a major mistake in drafting because there is no indication whatever within the Bill that that is the point. This is very important, Madam Speaker. At the present time domestic producers in the textile and clothing industry have the right to go to the Textile and Clothing Board and to take to that board complaints which are non-safeguard action complaints. If the Minister intends to apply this safeguard action test, that will, in fact, take away from our domestic textile and clothing firms the right to be able to take complaints, as they have always done in the past to the Textile and Clothing Board, to this new international trade tribunal.
If that is the case, Madam Speaker, then the textile and clothing producers will not just have lost the right to see the Textile and Clothing Board initiate inquiries, they will not just have seen the Textile and Clothing Board lose the right to make recommendations, but they themselves will have lost the right to be able to take anything before this new international trade tribunal except those matters which are related to safeguard actions. Of course, safeguard actions are themselves only one sub-set of the kinds of activities which, as a result of injury, textile and clothing firms might wish to carry forward to this trade tribunal.
I recognize that these are technical issues which are difficult to deal with especially at this stage of the session, but I hope very much that the Minister will recognize, for the textile and clothing producers particularly, that this right to take their complaints to the new international trade tribunal is an important right which they have always had with respect to the Textile and Clothing Board. If we wipe it out, it will be an unfortunate and sad result for the textile and clothing manufacturers and workers of this country.

Madam Speaker, let me speak to these two motions. The first one was originally in the name of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) and is now moved by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). The second one is in the name of the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon).
The first one astonished me. The second I think is unnecessary. I know it is unnecessary but I think the best way to summarize my complaint is that it is redundant and not needed to accomplish the purpose to which the Hon. Member is speaking.
Let me speak to the first motion. In terms of a single producer having trouble with imports and wanting inquiries to be conducted, to argue that no inquiry could ever be conducted, of course, will not necessarily be the case at all. The new tribunal will be able to do general economic inquiries, conduct tariff-related inquiries and injury inquiries. It will have the responsibility for all injury inquiries, as the House knows.
In addition, the Government will be able to direct the tribunal to inquire into the injurious impact of imports which are not dumped or subsidized. The Government currently has the authority to request such inquiries under the Special Import Measures Act and in the case of textile and clothing products, under the Textile and Clothing Board Act.
The key problem with Motion No. 8 is that one sole producer could trigger what the Hon. Member is asking for. That is as protectionist a device as I have ever heard in this House from a Party which purports to believe in liberalized trade around the world. Just one producer, Madam Speaker. GATT, decades ago, threw out that standard as being nothing more than a standard of harassment, and is this the Liberal Party's position on this trade tribunal? I find that astonishing and I am very surprised-I have great respect for the Hon. Member for Trinity-that she would bring that motion forward.
This amendment would allow direct access to the tribunal by a single producer. I know why the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor does not support it, because it is so dangerously protectionist that it would hurt our reputation as supporters for liberalized trade around the world. For a Party to propose this amendment that says it does not believe in the free trade agreement with the United States but does believe in GATT and liberalized free trade, I find, is inconceivable and I will remind Liberal Members of it in the future.
Members who participated in the committee know that there was extensive discussion about what proportion of the industry should be represented in a petition. That was a serious question and we had a good discussion. I think everybody learned from it. The Government agreed to what it believed was a consensus on the concept. Instead of saying "a majority of producers" we agreed that "a major proportion of producers" should be able to have direct access to the tribunal, and the Bill before the House has been so amended.

I must ask the House, in the name of GATT as well as in the name of liberalized trade around the world, to defeat that proposed amendment. I think I am supported by members of the New Democratic Party on that.
Motion No. 9 is only about safeguard actions. I hasten to tell my hon. friend that that is what this Bill is about and that is what this particular clause is about.
It doesn't say so.

The amendment set out is intended to exclude from the definition of industry those producers who are related to importers or exporters of the goods in question. I know what is behind this question. This would give us a framework within which it would be possible for the new International Trade Tribunal to deal with some of the pressures and threats which we will face in the future. It would not be a protectionist framework in itself. Rather, it would require the tribunal, in analysing what it is undertaking, to assess very broadly the state of the industry and the impact that imports are having on it and, in considerable detail, to analyse the points which bear on the state of that industry itself. It seems to me that the narrow formulations of the past have not in fact given to our industries a sufficient safeguard against sudden thrusts from low-wage countries which undercut the jobs of Canadians and affect their families and communities.
Second, the amendment recognizes what the Bill does not recognize. The Bill has made a serious mistake in not recognizing that, for most industries, GATT and the GATT regime is what constitutes the framework within which there are certain obligations. There are also certain other goods which are outside GATT obligations, as, for instance, those goods which we used in our retaliation against the United States on the shakes and shingles case.
Most important, there is a class of very important goods in Canada which is not subject to GATT obligations but is, instead, a subject of the Arrangement Regarding International Trade in Textiles. In Canada, over 100,000 employees work in the clothing industry. I would venture to guess that close to
90,000	employees are working in the textile industry. These industries are located in small communities.
The potential impact on those firms is very serious. That is why we have seen at the international level the establishment of a completely separate regime with respect to textiles. It is why, in the trade tribunal and the clause which deals with domestic complaints, we should also recognize that some of those complaints may be brought by the textile and clothing industries, complaints which should be analysed with consideration, not to our obligations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, but instead with respect to our obligations under the Arrangement Regarding International Trade in Textiles.
If this amendment is accepted, we will see before us a much better Bill, a Bill which, first, does consider all economic factors which are important for an industry, and also recognizes the significant distinction which exists in the case of trade between those obligations we have under GATT and those obligations which affect the textile industry producers, workers, communities and people.

Madam Speaker, the amendment to Clause 27 in Motion No. 11 would, quite frankly, further twist the intent of the legislation. This was the import of what the Hon. Member was doing with the two previous motions as well. There would not be a requirement any longer that increased imports be the principal cause of serious injury. However, that is what this whole Bill is about.

Increased imports is the principal cause of serious injury. With any lower test than that, the system would degenerate into one used for nothing more than harassment, and Canada could quickly be called to explain itself by our major trading partners. It is a chauvinistic kind of approach.
We are members of GATT and this totally undercuts GATT. The Hon. Member opposite is proposing that the injury criteria be embodied in the legislation. The injury criteria are similar to those used in dumping and countervail inquiries and are incorporated in the rules of the Canadian Import Tribunal. Because injury criteria are not exhaustive and never can be, and are subject to constant multilateral negotiations, it is the Government's intention to include them in the rules of the tribunal.
I do not think I need say more. Those are the fundamental reasons why this amendment is not acceptable.

18 at page 13 the following:

Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act
"(2) Where, as a result of an inquiry, the Tribunal determines that the goods that are the subject matter of the inquiry are being imported in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic producers of like or directly competitive goods, the tribunal shall make a written report to the Minister setting out the results of the inquiry and containing a recommendation as to whether, in its opinion, special measures of protection should be implemented.
(3) The report of the Tribunal made pursuant to subsection (2) shall specify the recommended scope and duration of the special measures and shall be published in the Canada Gazette."

Madam Speaker, Motion No. 10 deals with the reporting powers of the tribunal. As the Bill presently stands, the new tribunal will not have the right to make recommendations to the Government for action in light of a finding of serious injury. Members of Parliament suggested during the course of the meeting of the legislative committee that the tribunal should have the right to make recommendations. However, to give the tribunal an automatic power to make recommendations would, the Minister stated, be tantamount to an abdication of the Government's policymaking responsibilities.
This is a strange fear. Even if the tribunal makes a recommendation, the Government will still have the power to reject or act upon it. Recommendations are essential. At least they provide some guidance to officials and the Government. One questions why the Government is opposed to even hearing a recommendation on an injury finding from an expert body like the proposed tribunal. The amendment would ensure that recommendations are reported by the tribunal and published in The Canada Gazette.

Madam Speaker, with respect to Motion No. 13, I want to point out to the Minister that, contrary to his constant refrain that we are trying to escape from our GATT obligations, we make quite clear in Motion No. 13 that we wish to add something to the Bill which will in turn make it quite clear that in making recommendations under this section, the tribunal shall consider Canada's obligations under GATT. We are making it quite clear that we are, have been and will continue to be a committed member of GATT.
The point that the Minister continues to miss is that these domestic complaints are not simply complaints brought under GATT. They will be brought by textile and clothing producers who are not subject to GATT, except for the special set of considerations established by GATT under its textile regime. These are separate and distinct from the obligations Canada has under GATT.
We have recommended that the tribunal, in making recommendations, shall consider Canada's obligations under GATT. We make it absolutely clear, but there are other parts of what will be undertaken by this tribunal which the Minister and his Department will recognize. Certainly some witnesses who testified before us in committee recognized them. The textile and clothing producers came before us, and the clothing workers communicated with us in writing, and indicated that they expect that, just as with the Textile and Clothing Board which is being amalgamated into this new tribunal, they will continue to have the right to bring forward complaints as domestic producers which will not fall under our GATT obligations but instead under our obligations under the various multi-fibre arrangements which have affected textiles, as I said, for 26 years.
As I pointed out to the Minister, there are a number of goods which he knows are not covered by GATT. Yet producers of those goods will also have the right to bring complaints before this tribunal. In those cases where they are not covered by GATT, surely the Minister is not saying he is going to impose GATT obligations on them? Surely he is not saying the same thing with respect to textiles and clothing? Despite the fact that they are not covered by GATT, he will, through this Bill, cover them under GATT. I think it is sheer nonsense for the Minister to put that into effect.
I would point out to him again that we are not talking about a single board, a special board which existed in the past, the Canadian Import Tribunal. We are talking about three tribunals, one of which, the Textile and Clothing Board, permitted domestic complaints from textile and clothing producers. Surely they will continue to have that right in the future. In doing so, it is simply inconceivable that they will be bound by GATT obligations when no other country forces its textile and clothing producers to be bound by GATT obligations. Surely the Minister is not trying to put our textile and clothing industries in much tighter strait-jackets than American, British, French and Italian textile producers. That does not make sense.
July 12, 1988

Madam Speaker, I hasten to respond to the Hon. Member on Motion No. 13. I think I have good news for him if he will listen carefully. The amendment set out in Motion No. 13 amplifies the provisions on the issue of recommendations and whether or not the tribunal should be making recommendations. The amendment goes further and requires the tribunal, in case of non-serious injury, to recommend the removal of preferential tariff concessions which are not obligations of Canada under the GATT.
We know that this amendment is targeting the general preferential tariff regime which Canada has in place. That is the concern of the Hon. Member. In the Government's view this provision is entirely unnecessary. The good news is that that Government now has a standing general reference to the Tariff Board on the GPT which will be given to the new CITT. This regime has operated satisfactorily in the past and there is no reason why it should not operate satisfactorily in the future.
The advantage of this is that if offers flexibility, given the future MTN negotiations and, more important, is less offensive to developing countries than would be a legislated obligation to remove the GPT. I would not want to have to go with our developing country friends with that legislative obligation. It should be part of a more flexible MTN negotiation. I ask the House again to reject these amendments.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to expedite debate, I did not intend to speak at the second reading stage of this Bill. However, after some conversations with the Minister, during which I had a few questions for him about financial institutions, I had the impression he would agree to respond to some of these questions which are related, though indirectly, to the Bill before the House. The Bill before the House today constitutes a request by a private company for a change in jurisdiction, that is, to have part of its operations, which were under federal jurisdiction, transferred to that section of the same group that was under the provincial jurisdiction of Quebec, and which in fact represented the majority of the assets of Montreal Trust.
After my conversations with the Minister and after reading the comments made by the President of Montreal Trust, Mr. Gratton, before the other honourable Chamber of this Parliament which examined the Bill in committee and heard witnesses, I was generally satisfied with what was said by the President of Montreal Trust, and I have no real problem with the Bill itself and its wording, so that as far as I was concerned, once the Minister answered some of my questions, clause-by-clause consideration could be done very quickly.
Madam Speaker, without being a cause for concern, and I am sure there are reasons, one does wonder why this is the third company that, for practical reasons, has expressed the desire to be transferred from a federal to a provincial charter. We had Les Cooperants in December 1987, TAlliance Industrielle a little earlier, and today, there are also rumours about La Sauvegarde and of course we have Montreal Trust.
When we look at how our financial institutions are evolving, we can say there have been various developments. First of all, we had a Green Paper, I think in April 1985, tabled by the former Minister responsible for financial institutions, which was examined by the Standing Committee on Finance

July 12, 1988
Montreal Trust Company of Canada
and Economic Affairs, under the distinguished chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Mississauga-South (Mr. Blencarn). This Committee did a considerable amount of work. It heard witnesses and reported to the House on developments in our financial institutions and on their ties outside the financial sector, with commercial and industrial sectors. The report also touched on issues such as the ownership of these institutions. Who may own or own shares in a bank or trust company or insurance company, and what percentage of the total share capital?
How many shares are in foreign hands? What are we supposed to do about issues such as selling insurance, and so forth? Quite a few quesitons were raised, especially in the subsequent document, the Blue Paper which was tabled, if I am not mistaken, in 1986. We had a report by the Commons Committee and the Senate Committee. We had a number of documents published by the Economic Council of Canada. All this goes back to 1985 and 1986.
The Minister tabled a Bill on financial institutions, which dealt with the restructuring of the role of the inspector of insurance companies, trust companies and banks, consolidating all these responsibilities under the same person. The Minister also tabled a Bill on certain conflicts of interest. Basically, however, there are a number of points that have yet to be dealt with, and which to a certain extent may lead financial institutions to consider a change to a federal or a provincial charter. I would like to ask the Minister whether the Government intends to table its Bill on ownership very shortly. We were informed some time ago that the Government felt that non-financial businesses should not be major shareholders in new financial firms. I am thinking of industrial and commercial groups that acquire a controlling interest in financial institutions or vice versa. I would like to ask the Minister whether the Government has reached a final decision in this respect. Will it be possible, in future, for financial institutions to be owned by commercial groups? I understand it was always agreed there would be a grandfather clause for existing groups.
Could the Minister inform the House what the Government's policy will be in this respect and when we can expect the appropiate legislation to be tabled?
