speechtext:
Madam Chairman, this particular set of questions does not relate directly to Bill S-17, but I will be happy to help the Hon. Member with his questions. As he knows, in December the Government released a draft Trust and Loans Companies Act which is really a boiler-plate or new model of legislation for insurance companies, banks, the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society, as well as trust and loans companies.
The reason we had the legislation released in draft form was to ensure that we had very intense consultations with the industry, not on hypothetical things but on the practicalities of the Bill. As a result of the consultations which have been very widespread with the provinces and industries, we have put
ourselves into a position whereby we can hasten the process of putting in place a new regime when the Bill comes into the House.
Frankly, this is the most important legislation ever in the history of Canada for restructuring our financial institutions and our financial system. Sweeping changes for the industry are proposed in it. I placed a great deal of importance on consultation. Because of the strategic importance of the financial institution industry in the country, we have to get it right and rather than present a Bill that was flawed and that had not had the benefit of proper consultation. We put forward a draft piece of legislation and encouraged consultation. During the period of talking to both industry and the provinces, numerous representations and many helpful suggestions were made upon which I am now acting.
As I noted in my press release on June 15, 1988, one of the constant themes throughout the consultations with both industry and the provinces was that the Government's over-all financial sector policy goals were applauded and supported, but it was felt that it could be accomplished with a lesser degree of reliance on the policy in that draft trust and loan legislation of separation of financial and commercial enterprises. It relied very heavily on that separation.
I am now investigating, as I said in that press release, whether any modifications in ownership policies should be made and whether the changes would require a strengthening of prudential rules. If we move back somewhat in our reliance upon the separation between commercial and financial links, then we should ask the question whether more prudential requirements are needed in the over-all legislation.
That is what we are examining now. We have virtually completed that examination. I expect to be in a position shortly to announce any changes. I remain committed to the notion and the commitment of moving the legislation ahead as quickly as possible while ensuring that the policy serves consumers and the industry well.
Introduction of the trust and loan legislation will be followed by changes to the Bank Act. After that the new insurance companies Bill and the Canadian Co-operative Credit Associations Bill will follow. That is a huge set of legislative changes. They will follow quickly because the thinking will have been done and the principles will have been revealed in the first Bill that is brought before the House.
We are resolved to move quickly. The new legislation will look different from the draft legislation because it will have less reliance on commercial financial links.

speechtext:
That is exactly the point that disturbs me. I have no problem with Bill S-17. In reviewing the testimony made before the Senate committee we see that it is a move by Montreal Trust that is based on sound business reasons. The fact remains that $4 billion worth of assets presently under federal jurisdiction will be moved to provincial jurisdiction. Out of this we will get a trust company with some $8 billion in assets.
What disturbs me is that policy is being made on the run. The Government has promised some action. Certainly it has been obvious from the types of failures of various trust companies we have seen in the 1980s that co-ordinated action was necessary. Basic agreements with the provinces were needed, in order that there was some sense of security in this country by depositors about where the financial institutions were going. I am afraid that there is still not a coherent set of policies nor a coherent set of federal-provincial agreements in order that depositors will know what is happening with our financial institutions.
The Minister stated that he is opposed to financial institutions such as trust companies selling insurance, and so are we. What the provinces are going to do nobody knows. We have moved $4 billion in assets with Bill S-17 from under federal jurisdiction to provincial jurisdiction that at some stage might allow-

And that might change. There is confusion. What we are doing today is making policy on the run. As John Lennon said, "Life is what happens to you while you are busy making other plans". The Government is busy making other plans, but life is going on, another $4 billion of assets are being moved over to a provincial jurisdiction, and we have no idea where that will lead to.
We have co-operated by allowing Bill S-17 to pass today in all stages in an easy manner. I wish to tell the Government that this is the last time. We will not allow other pieces of legislation like this one to go through as smoothly, without having the promised legislation from the Government and without having a coherent policy in this country. As we move to financial deregulation, having 10 or 11 different policies

with the federal Government not knowing quite where to go is not responsible government.

speechtext:
I am not too sure whether there is a question in all of that, but I am very anxious to reply. First, I do not think a federal Government has ever presented a more coherent or more comprehensive new set of principles for financial institutional reform than has this Government. The Blue Paper, the draft trust and loans legislation, is a blueprint the Hon. Member and the provinces can read if they want to know where the principals are going, and the provinces can also read. We would also like to do some fine tuning to maximize harmonization with the provinces.
I am very proud of the principles that we have laid down: to remove the barriers as much as possible among financial institutions, to allow capital to move, to allow ownership across the pillars, and to allow a great deal of one stop shopping. I am very proud of the new supervisory organization and procedures that have been put in place since Bill C-56 and Bill C-42. The reconstitution of the CDIC is all in place now and is off and running. Quite frankly the financial institutions in this country know where they stand. They never knew where they stood before. We want to maximize harmonization with the provinces. That is why we took a couple of extra months to do it, and I am very proud that we have.

speechtext:
I could not follow the thinking of the Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party, because the Hon. Minister had made it abundantly clear that insurance would not be sold by banks and trust companies, and properly so. Let the banks carry out their financial matters, and let the insurance companies carry out theirs. The Minister has been absolutely definite on that throughout the years. There is nothing wishy-washy about it. I commend the Minister on it, and 1 hope that he sticks to that policy, because it is a sound policy.
Since this comes under the Trust Companies Act, will there be any adverse effect at all on people in other provinces who have deposited money in the Montreal Trust Company?

subtopic: ACT TO AUTHORIZE THE CONTINUATION OF THE MONTREAL TRUST COMPAGNY OF CANADA MEASURE TO ENSURE CONTINUATION UNDER THE LAWS OF THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: I am very happy to respond to my hon. friend, and it is a responsible question. We have no reason to believe that in any way there would be any negative effect on depositors. As a matter of fact, they might find that life is clarified. Now there is an amalgamated institution that they are dealing with, and some of the overhead costs that were involved in running two institutions will be gone. Therefore they will probably have a slightly stronger institution that they are part of because they do not have to operate in two different jurisdictions. Depositors should feel confident, not the opposite.

speechtext:
The government Member took issue on the point I was attempting to make, that provincial Governments can have their own regulations dealing with trusts which might allow the sale of insurance. What we have done here is move $4 billion worth of assets under federal control to provincial
Montreal Trust Company of Canada
control. What the Province of Quebec will do in terms of its regulations we do not know. I am not certain what influence this Government will have on it.
I want to ask the Minister about another point. I think it is fair to say that Quebec has a pretty stringent and competent regulatory agency. We have not heard of too many financial institutions going Under in Quebec because of negligence in their regulatory agencies. Certainly we have seen this in other provinces.
Would the Government have facilitated this Bill had the request been, for example, to have it incorporated in Alberta or in Saskatchewan? In other words, what is your opinion of the Alberta regulatory agency?

speechtext: Madam Chairman, I think it is a first rule of Parliament that one does not ask hypothetical questions, let alone answer them. In fact, that question is not really appropriate. We have a situation in front of us with a good jurisdiction, which can do more than an adequate job with depositors' funds, and that is our concern.

subtopic: ACT TO AUTHORIZE THE CONTINUATION OF THE MONTREAL TRUST COMPAGNY OF CANADA MEASURE TO ENSURE CONTINUATION UNDER THE LAWS OF THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to come back to the question that was raised by the Member for Bow River concerning depositors. I agree with the Minister when he says that this should in no way affect the quality of the financial institution, all the more so since a financial institution that is under provincial jurisdiction still has the obligation of reporting to each of the provinces from which it obtains a licence to operate. Because a company that is registered or incorporated under the laws of Ontario, Quebec, or Alberta, and wants to do business in another province, must obtain a licence to operate in that field of provincial jurisdiction and present quite lengthy reports to each of those provincial jurisdictions. This does not in any way, I think, affect the quality of deposits, it may even improve it, because transfers are now allowed, and the consolidated assets will be greater and will protect all depositors.
I would like to raise another point. I do not think the Minister answered me. Of coure I understand the need for a little electoral bombast, the urge to say that one will protect banks and insurance salesmen. I understand that. I can appreciate the Minister's objections and comments, and I agree that the distribution of insurance by specialized agents is a valid service for consumers, and that to a certain extent, if all of these agents were private businesses, it might affect that service. I have no quarrel with the Minister's objective, but by not acting and by not solving the problem, as my colleague for Regina East just said, we will see businesses moving to the jurisdiction of Ontario or Quebec or other Provinces where those activities are permitted. Then the Minister will swell his chest and say: we have prevented the sale of insurance in our federal institutions, in banks, but finally this will be done
